title: Contraception in Malaysia: the pill (pil perancang), implant, IUD, injection and the morning-after pill
desc: Which contraception works best, and which suits you? How the implant, coil, injection, pill and condoms compare, their side effects, how to use the morning-after pill, the common myths, and where to get contraception in Malaysia, from LPPKN clinics to pharmacies.
headings: How well each method works · Long-acting methods: implant, coil and injection · The pill (pil perancang) · Condoms · The morning-after pill and emergency contraception · Common myths · Where to get contraception in Malaysia
keywords: Women's health Contraception Contraception Pil perancang Emergency contraception darah tinggi hypertension bp tekanan darah payudara kanser cancer mammogram pink october mengandung hamil pregnancy antenatal kecemasan emergency a&e hospital klinik doctor doktor gp aesthetic estetik kecantikan beauty kulit skin botox filler laser facial
body: The implant and the coil (IUD) are the most effective methods, at more than 99% in everyday use, because there is nothing to remember. The pill is more than 99% effective if taken perfectly, but about 91% in everyday use, because pills get missed. Only condoms protect against sexually transmitted infections, including HIV. The morning-after pill works best taken as soon as possible after unprotected sex, within 3 to 5 days depending on the type. In Malaysia, a pharmacist can supply levonorgestrel emergency pills without a doctor’s prescription. LPPKN’s Klinik Nur Sejahtera offer counselling, pills, injections, implants and coils at low fees, as do Klinik Kesihatan and private clinics. Method Everyday use How long it lasts Implant Over 99% 3 years Hormonal coil (IUS) Over 99% 3 to 8 years, depending on type Copper coil (IUD) Over 99% 5 to 10 years, depending on type Injection 94% Every 8 to 13 weeks (usually every 3 months) Combined pill or progestogen-only pill 91% Taken every day Male condom 82% Each time you have sex Fertility awareness (tracking your cycle) About 76% Daily tracking Withdrawal About 78% Each time “Everyday use” figures, from the NHS and US CDC, allow for real-life mistakes such as missed pills. With perfect use, the pill, injection and condoms all work much better. In Malaysia: the national Population and Family Survey found that in 2014 only about a third of married women aged 15 to 49 used a modern method. LPPKN figures for 2022 suggest about 1 in 4 women who want to avoid or delay pregnancy have an unmet need for contraception. Implant A small, flexible rod about the size of a matchstick, placed under the skin of the upper arm through a tiny cut after a local anaesthetic. It takes a few minutes. Releases a progestogen hormone and is licensed for 3 years. It can be removed at any time, and fertility returns quickly. The most common side effect is changes to periods : they may become lighter, stop, or become irregular or longer. There isn’t good evidence that it causes weight gain. A 2023 study of Ministry of Health clinics found the implant was the most cost-effective method they offered. Coil (IUD and IUS) A small T-shaped device placed in the womb by a trained doctor or nurse. The copper coil has no hormones, works straight away, lasts 5 to 10 years, and can also be used as emergency contraception. Periods may become heavier or more painful at first. The hormonal coil lasts 3 to 8 years and usually makes periods lighter and less painful. See our guide to period pain . Fertility returns as soon as it is removed. Injection A progestogen injection every 8 to 13 weeks, usually every 3 months. Periods often stop. Some people gain weight, and it can thin the bones slightly with long use, which recovers after stopping. It can take up to a year for fertility to return after stopping, so it may not suit you if you plan to get pregnant soon. The combined pill contains oestrogen and progestogen. It is taken daily, usually for 21 days followed by a 7-day break, or every day with dummy pills. If you start it on day 1 to 5 of your period, it protects you straight away. Otherwise use condoms for the first 7 days. Benefits: periods are often lighter, more regular and less painful, and it can help acne. It lowers the risk of womb, ovarian and bowel cancer. Side effects: spotting, headaches, nausea, sore breasts and mood changes, which often settle within a few months. There is no good evidence that it causes weight gain. Risks: a small increased risk of blood clots, and a slight increase in breast and cervical cancer risk while taking it, which returns to normal 10 years after stopping. It may not suit you if you smoke and are 35 or over, have migraine with aura, high blood pressure, a history of blood clots, stroke or heart disease, are very overweight, or have had breast cancer. A doctor will check your health and blood pressure before prescribing it. Missed pills: if you are less than 48 hours late with one combined pill, take it as soon as you remember and carry on. If you have missed two or more, follow the leaflet in your pack, use condoms for 7 days, and ask a pharmacist whether you need emergency contraception. The progestogen-only pill (“mini-pill”) has no oestrogen, so it suits more people, including those who are breastfeeding, smoke or can’t take oestrogen. It is taken every day without a break, and needs to be taken at the same time each day. For women with PCOS, the pill can also help with irregular periods, acne and excess hair: see our guide to PCOS (PMOS) . Condoms are the only method that also protects against sexually transmitted infections, including HIV, syphilis and gonorrhoea. Many people use them alongside another method for extra protection. Use a new one every time, check the expiry date, and use water-based lubricant with latex condoms. See our guides to STI testing and HIV and PrEP . If you have had sex without contraception, or your method failed (for example, a split condom or missed pills), emergency contraception can prevent pregnancy: Option Take or fit within Notes Levonorgestrel pill 72 hours (3 days) Works best the sooner it is taken. May work less well in people weighing more than about 70 kg Ulipristal pill 120 hours (5 days) More effective than levonorgestrel later in the 5 days Copper coil 5 days The most effective option, over 99%, and then gives ongoing contraception Emergency pills work by delaying ovulation. They don’t cause an abortion and won’t harm an existing pregnancy. In Malaysia, levonorgestrel emergency pills are classed so that a pharmacist can supply them without a doctor’s prescription , after a short consultation. Ask the pharmacist about other options, which may need a doctor. If you vomit within a few hours of taking the pill, ask a pharmacist or doctor whether to take another. Do a pregnancy test if your next period is more than 7 days late or unusually light. Emergency contraception isn’t meant for regular use. Talk to a doctor or LPPKN clinic about an ongoing method. “Contraception causes infertility.” No. Fertility returns soon after stopping the pill, implant or coil. After the injection it can take several months, up to a year. “The pill makes you fat.” Studies haven’t shown that the pill causes significant weight gain. The injection is the method most linked to weight gain. “You don’t need contraception after 40.” You can still get pregnant until menopause, so contraception is still needed. “The morning-after pill is an abortion pill.” No. It prevents or delays ovulation and doesn’t end a pregnancy. LPPKN (Klinik Nur Sejahtera): family planning counselling, pills, injections, implants and coils. Fees are low: for example, RM5 registration and RM10 consultation, with pills from RM5, the injection RM36, and implant insertion RM500, according to LPPKN’s fee list updated in June 2026. LPPKN also gives free contraceptives to eligible B40 women. Klinik Kesihatan: government health clinics offer the pill, injection, coil and implant. Private GP and women’s clinics: you can usually be seen quickly, including for implant and coil fitting. Call ahead to check which methods they offer. Pharmacies: condoms, and emergency contraception after a consultation with the pharmacist. Ongoing pills need a doctor’s assessment first. FRHAM (Federation of Reproductive Health Associations, Malaysia) state associations also provide contraception and sexual health services. Unmarried women: doctors and health researchers say the Ministry of Health has no policy against providing contraception to unmarried women, but some women have reported being turned away or asked for a marriage certificate. Practice varies between clinics, so it may be worth calling ahead. What is the most effective contraception? The implant and the coil (hormonal or copper) are more than 99% effective in everyday use, because there is nothing to remember. How effective is the pill? More than 99% if taken perfectly, but about 91% in everyday use, because pills are sometimes missed or taken late. Can I buy the morning-after pill without a prescription in Malaysia? Yes, levonorgestrel emergency pills can be supplied by a pharmacist without a doctor’s prescription, after a short consultation. How long after sex can I take the morning-after pill? Levonorgestrel within 72 hours and ulipristal within 120 hours, but the sooner the better. A copper coil fitted within 5 days is the most effective option. How long does the implant last? It is licensed for 3 years, and can be removed at any time if you want to get pregnant or switch methods. Does contraception cause infertility? No. Fertility returns soon after stopping most methods. After the injection it can take several months, up to a year. Where can I get contraception in Malaysia? At LPPKN’s Klinik Nur Sejahtera, Klinik Kesihatan, private GP and women’s clinics, and, for condoms and emergency pills, pharmacies. Does the pill protect against STIs? No. Only condoms protect against sexually transmitted infections, including HIV.

title: Period pain (senggugut): what’s normal, what helps, and signs of endometriosis or fibroids
desc: Three in four Malaysian schoolgirls have period pain, and most never see a doctor. What helps (and when to take it), the signs that pain isn’t “normal” and could be endometriosis, fibroids or adenomyosis, and how to tell normal discharge (keputihan) from an infection.
headings: What causes period pain? · What helps period pain (cara hilangkan senggugut) · Hormonal treatment · When period pain isn’t “normal” · Endometriosis · Fibroids and adenomyosis · Vaginal discharge (keputihan): what’s normal? · Period pain, school and work
keywords: Women's health Period pain (senggugut) Dysmenorrhoea Senggugut Endometriosis denggi aedes nyamuk mosquito mengandung hamil pregnancy antenatal aesthetic estetik kecantikan beauty kulit skin botox filler laser facial
body: About 3 in 4 secondary schoolgirls in Kuala Lumpur and Kelantan studies had period pain, and more than 1 in 5 of those in Kuala Lumpur missed school because of it. Few saw a doctor. Anti-inflammatory painkillers (NSAIDs) such as ibuprofen, naproxen or mefenamic acid work best, started at the first sign of a period or a day before. They work better than paracetamol. Heat, such as a heat pad or hot water bottle, may work about as well as painkillers. Regular exercise also helps. Hormonal contraception, such as the pill, implant or hormonal coil, can greatly reduce period pain. See a doctor if pain is getting worse, isn’t helped by painkillers, stops you doing daily activities, or comes with heavy periods, bleeding between periods or pain during sex. Primary dysmenorrhoea is ordinary period pain with no underlying disease. It is caused by the womb muscle tightening to shed its lining, driven by chemicals called prostaglandins. It usually starts within a few years of the first period, begins just before or as bleeding starts, and lasts up to 3 days. It often improves with age and after childbirth. Secondary dysmenorrhoea is pain caused by a condition such as endometriosis, adenomyosis, fibroids or pelvic infection. It often starts later in life, gets worse over time, or lasts beyond the first days of bleeding. A copper coil can also make periods more painful in the first few months. In Malaysia: in a study of more than 1,000 secondary schoolgirls in Kuala Lumpur, 74.5% had period pain. Of these, 21.5% missed school and about half found it hard to concentrate in class, yet only 12% had seen a doctor. A similar study in rural Kelantan found 76% had period pain. Painkillers (ubat senggugut) Anti-inflammatory painkillers (NSAIDs) , such as ibuprofen, naproxen or mefenamic acid, block the prostaglandins that cause the pain. A Cochrane review found about half of women got good relief, against 18% with a dummy pill, and NSAIDs worked better than paracetamol. Timing matters: start at the first sign of your period, or a day before if your periods are regular, and take them regularly for the first 2 to 3 days rather than waiting until the pain is bad. Take them with food. Don’t take NSAIDs if you have a stomach ulcer, kidney problems, some types of asthma, or suspected dengue . Paracetamol is an alternative. Ask a pharmacist if unsure. Heat: a heat pad, heat patch, hot water bottle or warm bath on the lower tummy or back. A 2026 review of 57 trials found heat may relieve period pain about as well as NSAIDs, with fewer side effects. Exercise: regular exercise, such as brisk walking, yoga or aerobics about 3 times a week, reduced period pain in a Cochrane review. Gentle movement during your period can help too. Other options: a TENS machine (a small device that sends mild electrical pulses through the skin) may help a little. Ginger has been studied in small trials, with some benefit, but the evidence is weak. Not smoking and cutting down on alcohol can also help. Anti-inflammatory painkillers work best when started at the very start of your period. If painkillers and heat aren’t enough, hormonal contraception can make periods lighter and much less painful, and is often a first choice for women who also want contraception: the combined pill , which can also be taken back-to-back to have fewer periods the hormonal coil (IUS), which reduces both pain and heavy bleeding the implant or progestogen-only pill See our guide to contraception in Malaysia . A doctor will usually review how you are doing after about 3 months. See a doctor if: your periods are becoming more painful , heavier or irregular pain stops you going to school or work, or isn’t helped by painkillers taken properly you have pain during or after sex you have pain passing urine or opening your bowels during your period, or bowel or bladder changes you have bleeding between periods or after sex your periods are very heavy : changing a pad every 1 to 2 hours, bleeding for more than 7 days, passing large clots, flooding, or feeling tired and breathless (signs of anaemia) you have had pelvic infections before, have a family history of endometriosis, or are having difficulty getting pregnant Get urgent help for sudden, severe pelvic pain, especially with fever, fainting, or if you could be pregnant. Endometriosis is when tissue similar to the womb lining grows outside the womb, for example on the ovaries and pelvic lining, causing inflammation, pain and scarring. It affects about 1 in 10 women of reproductive age worldwide, and Malaysian specialists give similar estimates. Symptoms include very painful periods, pain during sex, pelvic pain at other times, pain opening the bowels, tiredness, and difficulty getting pregnant. Diagnosis is often delayed by years: worldwide, 4 to 12 years on average. Malaysian patient groups report women being told their pain is normal. A normal ultrasound or MRI doesn’t rule it out . The definite test is a keyhole operation (laparoscopy), which can also remove the tissue. There is no cure, but treatment with painkillers, hormonal medicines and surgery can control symptoms well, and fertility treatment can help women trying to conceive. Fibroids are non-cancerous growths in or on the womb. Many cause no symptoms, but they can cause heavy or painful periods, pressure on the bladder or bowel, and iron-deficiency anaemia. Adenomyosis is when the womb lining grows into the muscle wall of the womb. It is more common after 35 and after having children, and causes painful, heavy periods. Both are usually found on an ultrasound. Treatment ranges from painkillers, medicine to reduce bleeding and hormonal treatment to procedures and surgery, depending on your symptoms and whether you want children. Heavy periods can cause anaemia: see our guide to blood test results . Irregular periods with acne or excess hair may point to PCOS (PMOS) instead. Some vaginal discharge is normal and healthy. It keeps the vagina clean. Normal: clear or white, thin and slippery or thick and sticky, with no strong smell. It changes through your cycle and is often wetter and stretchier around ovulation. Change Possible cause Thin, grey-white, fishy smell Bacterial vaginosis Thick, white, like cottage cheese, with itching Thrush (yeast infection) Green, yellow or frothy Trichomoniasis With pelvic pain, bleeding or pain passing urine Chlamydia or gonorrhoea See a doctor if your discharge changes in colour, smell or amount, or comes with itching, soreness, pain or bleeding. Don’t douche or use perfumed washes inside the vagina, which upset its natural balance. See our guides to STI testing , UTIs and the Pap smear and HPV test . Malaysia has no separate law on menstrual leave. The government said in 2022 that period leave would need further study, and no policy has followed. If period pain stops you working, a doctor can assess you and decide whether to issue an MC. See our guide to medical certificates . If you regularly miss school or work because of period pain, that is a reason to see a doctor, as treatment usually helps. What is senggugut in English? Senggugut is period pain, also called menstrual cramps or dysmenorrhoea. What is the best medicine for period pain? Anti-inflammatory painkillers (NSAIDs) such as ibuprofen, naproxen or mefenamic acid, started at the first sign of your period and taken regularly for the first 2 to 3 days. Paracetamol is an alternative if you can’t take NSAIDs. How can I relieve period pain without medicine? Heat on the lower tummy or back, such as a heat pad or hot water bottle, gentle exercise, a warm bath and massage. Regular exercise through the month also helps. Is severe period pain normal? Some pain is common, but pain that stops you going to school or work, isn’t helped by painkillers or is getting worse should be checked by a doctor. What are the signs of endometriosis? Very painful periods, pain during sex, pelvic pain at other times, pain opening your bowels during your period, and difficulty getting pregnant. Can the pill help period pain? Yes. The combined pill, hormonal coil and implant can make periods lighter and much less painful. What colour discharge is normal? Clear or white with no strong smell is normal. Grey with a fishy smell, thick and white with itching, or green, yellow or frothy discharge can mean an infection. Can I get an MC for period pain in Malaysia? There is no separate menstrual leave law. A doctor can assess you and decide whether to issue an MC if pain stops you working.

title: Kidney stones (batu karang): symptoms, treatment, and how to stop them coming back
desc: Kidney stone pain is one of the worst pains people describe. The symptoms, the danger signs that need a hospital straight away, which stones pass on their own, the treatments available in Malaysia, and the simple diet changes that cut the chance of another stone.
headings: What are kidney stones? · Symptoms of kidney stones (tanda batu karang) · How kidney stones are diagnosed · Treatment · How to stop stones coming back · Kidney stones vs gallstones (batu hempedu)
keywords: Guides Kidney stones (batu karang) Kidney stones Batu karang Urolithiasis kencing manis gula hba1c darah tinggi hypertension bp tekanan darah mengandung hamil pregnancy antenatal kecemasan emergency a&e hospital klinik doctor doktor gp saringan check-up checkup medical aesthetic estetik kecantikan beauty kulit skin botox filler laser facial
body: The typical symptom is severe pain in the side or lower back that comes in waves and spreads to the groin, often with nausea, vomiting or blood in the urine. Go to an emergency department for stone pain with fever or shivering, pain that painkillers don’t control, or if you can’t pass urine. About 3 in 4 stones smaller than 5 mm pass on their own, usually within a few weeks. Larger stones may need shock-wave treatment (ESWL), laser removal through a thin scope, or keyhole surgery. A Sarawak screening study found stones in about 4% of adults, and many people get another within 5 to 10 years. Drinking 2.5 to 3 litres of fluid a day, cutting salt and keeping a normal calcium intake are the most important ways to prevent stones. Kidney stones form when substances in the urine, such as calcium, oxalate and uric acid, become too concentrated and crystallise. They range from grains of sand to several centimetres across. Type How common Linked to Calcium stones (mostly calcium oxalate) Most stones Low fluid intake, high salt, high urine calcium or oxalate Uric acid About 1 in 10 Acidic urine, gout, diabetes, obesity. See our guide to gout and uric acid Struvite Less common Repeated urinary infections. They can grow quickly Cystine Rare An inherited condition In Malaysia: an ultrasound screening of more than 1,000 adults at clinics in Sarawak found kidney stones in about 4%, and 6.4% had had them at some point. Malaysian urologists point to the hot, humid climate and chronic dehydration as major contributors. Risk factors include not drinking enough, a family history of stones, being overweight, diabetes, gout, high blood pressure, bowel disease, repeated urinary infections and some medicines. Stones sitting in the kidney often cause no symptoms. Pain starts when a stone moves into the tube between the kidney and the bladder (the ureter): severe pain in the side or lower back , below the ribs, that comes in waves and may spread to the lower tummy or groin (renal colic) restlessness: people often can’t lie still nausea and vomiting blood in the urine , which may look pink, red or brown needing to pass urine often, or burning when you do Go to an emergency department straight away if you have: stone pain with a fever, chills or shivering . This can mean an infected, blocked kidney, which needs urgent drainage and antibiotics. pain that painkillers don’t control, or constant vomiting no urine, or only one working kidney Pain in the side with fever but no stone can be a kidney infection: see our guide to urinary tract infections . Severe pain on the lower right side may be appendicitis . A CT scan without contrast is the most accurate test and shows the size and position of the stone. An ultrasound is used first in pregnancy and in children, and is often used to check the kidneys for blockage. Urine and blood tests check for blood, infection and kidney function. See our guide to blood test results . If you pass a stone, try to catch it by passing urine through a sieve or tea strainer, and give it to your doctor. Knowing what it is made of helps prevent the next one. Small stones (under 5 mm): about 3 in 4 pass on their own, and more if they are already low in the ureter. This can take a few weeks. Pain relief: anti-inflammatory painkillers (NSAIDs) are the first choice, as long as your kidneys are working normally and you can take them safely. Drink enough to keep your urine pale, but don’t force down huge amounts. For stones of 5 to 10 mm low in the ureter, a doctor may prescribe a tablet (an alpha-blocker such as tamsulosin) to relax the ureter and help the stone pass. The benefit is modest. Larger stones, or stones that don’t pass: Treatment What it involves Usually for Shock-wave lithotripsy (ESWL) Shock waves from outside the body break the stone into fragments that pass in the urine. No cuts Kidney and some ureteric stones up to about 20 mm Ureteroscopy with laser (URS / RIRS) A thin scope is passed up through the urethra and bladder, and a laser breaks up the stone. Usually same-day discharge Ureteric stones, and kidney stones up to about 20 mm Percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) Keyhole surgery through a small cut in the back to remove the stone. A few days in hospital Large kidney stones, over 20 mm A small tube ( stent ) is sometimes left between the kidney and bladder for a few weeks after treatment, and removed later. Government hospitals with urology departments, such as Hospital Selayang, offer ESWL and laser treatment by referral. Be wary of “ubat batu karang” sold online with claims to dissolve stones. Most stones won’t dissolve, and relying on these can delay treatment while a blocked kidney is damaged. Unregistered products have also been linked to kidney damage. Check for a MAL registration number, and talk to your doctor or pharmacist first. Stones often come back: by some estimates about half of people get another within 5 to 10 years without prevention. European urology guidelines advise: Drink 2.5 to 3 litres of fluid a day , mainly water, enough to keep your urine pale. Drink more in hot weather, when working outdoors and after exercise. Cut down on salt to 4 to 5 g a day (less than a teaspoon), including salty sauces, processed food and instant noodles. Don’t cut out calcium. Normal calcium intake from food, such as milk, yoghurt and tofu, actually lowers the risk of calcium stones. Moderate animal protein (meat, chicken, seafood). Avoid sugary drinks. Adding fresh lemon or lime juice to water may help. Keep to a healthy weight. See our BMI calculator . Only cut down on high-oxalate foods, such as spinach and nuts, if tests show you have high oxalate levels. People who have had several stones, or are at high risk, may be offered urine tests over 24 hours and a stone analysis. Depending on the results, medicines can lower the risk of new stones. In Malaysia’s heat, drink more on days you are outdoors or exercising. Gallstones are a different condition. They form in the gallbladder , under the liver, and cause pain in the upper middle or upper right of the tummy, under the ribs, that can last from 30 minutes to several hours. Yellowing of the skin or eyes with gallstone pain needs urgent care. See our guide to stomach pain . What are the symptoms of kidney stones? Severe pain in the side or lower back that comes in waves and spreads to the groin, often with nausea, vomiting, blood in the urine or needing to pass urine often. Can kidney stones pass on their own? Yes, most small ones do. About 3 in 4 stones under 5 mm pass by themselves, usually within a few weeks. When is kidney stone pain an emergency? If you also have a fever, chills or shivering, if painkillers don’t control the pain, if you are vomiting constantly, or if you can’t pass urine. How are large kidney stones removed? With shock-wave treatment (ESWL), a thin scope and laser passed up through the urethra (ureteroscopy), or keyhole surgery through the back (PCNL) for large stones. How much water should I drink to prevent kidney stones? About 2.5 to 3 litres of fluid a day, mostly water, enough to keep your urine pale. More in hot weather or when sweating. Should I avoid calcium if I have kidney stones? No. A normal calcium intake from food lowers the risk of the most common stones. Cut down on salt instead. Do herbal remedies dissolve kidney stones? There is no good evidence that they do, and relying on them can delay treatment. Check any product is registered and ask your doctor first. What is the difference between kidney stones and gallstones? Kidney stones form in the urinary system and cause side or back pain. Gallstones form in the gallbladder and cause pain in the upper right or middle of the tummy.

title: Boils (bisul) and styes (ketumbit): causes, home care, draining, and when to see a doctor
desc: Boils and styes are common, painful and usually harmless. What causes them, how to care for them at home, why you shouldn’t squeeze them, when a doctor needs to drain one, and why boils that keep coming back are a reason to check your blood sugar.
headings: What is a boil (bisul)? · Caring for a boil at home · When to see a doctor about a boil · Boils that keep coming back · Styes (ketumbit) and chalazion
keywords: Aesthetics & skin Boils and styes Boil Bisul Stye kencing manis gula hba1c payudara kanser cancer mammogram pink october aesthetic estetik kecantikan beauty kulit skin botox filler laser facial
body: Boils and styes are caused by Staphylococcus aureus bacteria, which about 1 in 5 people carry harmlessly in the nose and on the skin. A warm, clean compress for about 10 minutes several times a day helps a boil or stye come to a head and drain. Most boils heal in about 10 days, and most styes within a week. Don’t squeeze, pierce or cut a boil or stye. It can push the infection deeper, especially on the face. See a doctor for a boil on the face, a large or very painful boil, fever, spreading redness, a cluster of boils (carbuncle), or a stye that affects your vision or causes eyelid swelling. Boils that keep coming back can be a sign of undiagnosed diabetes. About 2 in 5 Malaysian adults with diabetes don’t know they have it. A boil (furuncle) is a deep infection of a hair follicle. It starts as a tender red lump, which swells and fills with pus over a few days, and usually forms a yellow or white head before bursting and draining. A carbuncle is a cluster of boils joined together under the skin, often on the back of the neck, shoulders or thighs. It is more likely to cause fever and needs a doctor. Cause: the bacterium Staphylococcus aureus . About 10 to 20% of people carry it, mostly in the nose, armpits and groin. It gets into the skin through small cuts, grazes, insect bites, or friction from tight clothing and sweat. More likely if you have diabetes, are overweight, have eczema, a weak immune system or iron deficiency, smoke, or live with someone who gets boils. Warm compress: hold a clean cloth soaked in warm (not hot) water on the boil for about 10 minutes, up to 4 times a day. This eases the pain and helps it come to a head and drain on its own. Don’t squeeze, pick or pierce it , and don’t cut it open yourself. This can push the infection deeper or spread it. Once it drains, wash gently with soap and water, and cover it with a clean dressing until it heals. Wash your hands after touching it. Use your own towel, and wash towels, bedding and clothes on a hot wash. Take paracetamol or ibuprofen for pain if needed. Avoid swimming pools and shared gym equipment until it has healed. Most boils heal within about 10 days. See a doctor the same day if: the boil is on your face , especially around the nose and upper lip. Veins here connect to the inside of the skull, so infection can rarely spread there, and squeezing makes it more likely. the skin around it is red, hot, swollen and spreading (cellulitis) you have a fever , chills or feel unwell it is very large or very painful, or you have a carbuncle you have diabetes or a weak immune system See a GP if a boil hasn’t got better after 2 weeks, or you keep getting boils. Treatment: under the Ministry of Health’s antimicrobial guideline, the main treatment for a boil or abscess full of pus is drainage : the doctor numbs the skin, makes a small cut to let the pus out, and dresses the wound. Antibiotics aren’t needed for most simple boils, but are used for large or spreading infections, carbuncles, fever, facial boils, or if drainage alone hasn’t worked. The doctor may send a swab to check which antibiotics work, as some staph bacteria (MRSA) are resistant to common ones. Check your blood sugar. Poorly controlled diabetes makes boils more common and slower to heal. In Malaysia, 15.6% of adults have diabetes and about 2 in 5 of them don’t know it. See our guide to normal blood sugar levels . Clearing the bacteria: for repeated boils, a doctor may suggest an antiseptic nasal ointment and an antiseptic body wash for a few days, sometimes for everyone in the household, along with washing towels and bedding. Painful lumps that keep coming back in the armpits, groin or under the breasts , with blackheads and scarring, may be hidradenitis suppurativa , a long-term inflammatory skin condition rather than ordinary boils. It needs a doctor or dermatologist. Boils that keep coming back are a good reason to have your blood sugar checked. A stye (hordeolum, ketumbit ) is a painful red lump on the edge of the eyelid, caused by bacteria infecting an eyelash follicle or eyelid gland. It usually goes away within a week. A chalazion is a usually painless, firm lump further back on the eyelid, caused by a blocked oil gland. It can follow a stye and may last for weeks. Home care: Hold a clean, warm cloth against the closed eye for 5 to 10 minutes, 3 or 4 times a day, then gently massage the area. Don’t squeeze or burst it , and don’t pull out the eyelashes. Don’t wear eye make-up or contact lenses until it has healed, and throw away old eye make-up. Keep your eyelids clean, especially if you have dandruff or blepharitis (inflamed eyelid edges), which make styes more likely. Antibiotics usually aren’t needed. A Cochrane review found no good evidence that they help an ordinary stye. A doctor may prescribe them if the infection is spreading. The old belief that a stye comes from peeking at something you shouldn’t have is just a myth. Styes are caused by bacteria, often carried from the nose to the eye on unwashed fingers. See a doctor if: the stye doesn’t improve after a week or two, your vision is affected, the whole eyelid or the skin around the eye becomes red and swollen, the eye itself is red and painful, or styes keep coming back. A chalazion that lasts may need a small procedure to drain it. For a red, sticky eye, see our guide to conjunctivitis . What is bisul in English? Bisul is a boil, a painful pus-filled lump caused by a bacterial infection of a hair follicle. How do I get rid of a boil fast? Hold a warm compress on it for about 10 minutes up to 4 times a day to help it drain. Don’t squeeze it. See a doctor if it is large, very painful, on your face, or you have a fever. Should I squeeze a boil? No. Squeezing can push the infection deeper or spread it, especially on the face. A doctor can drain it safely if needed. Do boils need antibiotics? Most simple boils don’t. Large or spreading infections, carbuncles, facial boils, fever, or boils in people with diabetes or a weak immune system may need antibiotics. Why do I keep getting boils? Common reasons include carrying staph bacteria in the nose, diabetes, friction and sweat, or close contact with others who get boils. See a doctor to check your blood sugar and discuss clearing the bacteria. What is ketumbit in English? Ketumbit is a stye, a small painful infection on the edge of the eyelid. How long does a stye last? Usually about a week. Warm compresses help it drain. See a doctor if it lasts longer than a week or two or affects your vision. What is the difference between a stye and a chalazion? A stye is a painful infection at the eyelid edge. A chalazion is a usually painless lump further back on the eyelid from a blocked oil gland, which can last for weeks.

title: Warts (ketuat): types, treatment at home and at a clinic, and when to see a doctor
desc: Warts are harmless growths caused by a virus, and many disappear on their own. The different types, how they spread, home treatments that work if you stick with them, freezing and other clinic treatments, and the warts you should never treat yourself.
headings: Types of warts · How warts spread · Treating warts at home (ubat ketuat) · Clinic treatments · When to see a doctor · Preventing warts
keywords: Aesthetics & skin Warts (ketuat) Warts Ketuat Plantar wart kencing manis gula hba1c vaksin suntikan jab immunisation klinik doctor doktor gp aesthetic estetik kecantikan beauty kulit skin botox filler laser facial
body: Warts are caused by HPV entering through small breaks in the skin. They spread by touch and on wet surfaces such as shower floors, but aren’t very contagious. Half of children’s warts go away within a year and two-thirds within two years without treatment. Salicylic acid from a pharmacy works if used daily for up to 3 months. Freezing (cryotherapy) at a clinic is another option. Don’t treat warts on the face or genitals yourself, and check with a doctor first if you have diabetes or poor circulation. See a doctor if a growth bleeds, changes, hurts or you aren’t sure it is a wart. Type Where What it looks like Common wart Fingers, hands, knees, elbows Firm, rough, raised bump, often with tiny black dots (clotted blood vessels) Plantar wart (verruca) Soles of the feet Flat, hard patch pushed into the skin by walking, often painful, with black dots Flat (plane) wart Face, backs of hands, legs Small, smooth, slightly raised, often in groups. Shaving can spread them Filiform wart Face, around the mouth and nose Thin, finger-like growth Periungual wart Around the fingernails and toenails Rough growths that can affect nail growth Genital warts Genitals and anus Small, soft lumps. Caused by different HPV types, mostly passed on through sex Plantar wart or corn? Plantar warts are sometimes called mata ikan because of their black dots. Corns and calluses are thickened skin from pressure or rubbing, often from tight shoes, and aren’t caused by a virus. If the hard skin is gently pared down, a wart shows tiny black dots while a corn doesn’t. by direct skin contact, or by touching surfaces such as towels, shoes, and wet floors around pools and showers from one part of your own body to another, for example by picking, biting nails or shaving over warts more easily when the skin is wet, soft or damaged A wart can take weeks to months to appear after contact. Children and teenagers get them most, as do people with eczema or a weak immune system. Genital warts are a sexually transmitted infection, usually caused by HPV types 6 and 11. They spread through skin-to-skin contact during sex, even when no warts are visible, but not through towels or toilet seats. They need a doctor. See our guide to STI testing . Treatment isn’t essential, as many warts go away on their own: half of children’s warts within a year, and two-thirds within two years. If a wart is painful, spreading or bothering you, these options from a pharmacy can help: Salicylic acid (gel, paint or plaster) is the best-studied home treatment. In a Cochrane review it worked better than a dummy treatment. Soak the wart in warm water for a few minutes, then dry it. Gently rub away the dead surface skin with a pumice stone or emery board. Use it only for the wart, and don’t share it. Apply the treatment only to the wart , protecting the skin around it, once a day. Keep going for up to 12 weeks . Stopping early is the commonest reason it fails. Take a few days off if the skin becomes sore. Freezing sprays sold in pharmacies are weaker than clinic freezing and aren’t suitable for young children. Don’t use home treatments : on the face , genitals or broken skin if you have diabetes , poor circulation or numbness in your feet, without a doctor’s advice Never cut, burn or dig out a wart yourself. Be careful with “wart remover” products sold online. Check that the product is registered with the National Pharmaceutical Regulatory Agency (NPRA), and stop if it causes pain, bleeding or blistering. Treatment What it involves Cryotherapy (freezing) Liquid nitrogen is applied to freeze the wart. It stings and usually blisters, then the wart falls off within a week or so. Several sessions, 2 to 4 weeks apart, are often needed. Not usually used in young children Curettage and cautery The wart is scraped away under local anaesthetic and the base sealed with heat. Can leave a scar Laser For stubborn warts that haven’t responded to other treatment Prescription creams and immunotherapy Medicines that irritate the wart or stimulate the immune system to clear it, mainly for stubborn or genital warts Freezing combined with salicylic acid may work better than salicylic acid alone. All treatments can leave small marks or pale or dark patches, and warts can come back. Freezing near the nails can damage the nail. Genital warts are treated by a doctor with prescription creams, freezing or other procedures. Don’t use pharmacy wart products on them. GP clinics and dermatologists can freeze or remove stubborn warts. the growth bleeds, changes in size, shape or colour, itches or hurts you aren’t sure it is a wart. Some skin cancers and other growths, such as seborrhoeic keratoses, can look similar. it is on your face or genitals, or you have many warts it keeps coming back or spreading, or home treatment hasn’t worked after 12 weeks you have diabetes, poor circulation or a weak immune system Don’t pick, scratch or bite warts, and don’t shave over them. Don’t share towels, shoes or socks. Wear flip-flops in shared showers and around pools, and cover verrucas with a waterproof plaster when swimming. Keep your feet dry and change socks daily. Vaccines covering HPV types 6 and 11 protect against most genital warts, and the HPV vaccine also prevents cervical and other cancers. Ask your doctor which vaccine you are being offered. See our guide to the HPV vaccine . What causes ketuat? Warts (ketuat) are caused by the human papillomavirus (HPV), which gets into the skin through small cuts or breaks. Do warts go away on their own? Often, yes. Half of children’s warts disappear within a year and two-thirds within two years. Adults’ warts can take longer. What is the best treatment for warts? Salicylic acid used every day for up to 12 weeks is the best-studied home treatment. Freezing at a clinic is an alternative, and the two can be combined. Are warts contagious? Mildly. They spread by touch and on wet surfaces such as shower floors, and you can spread them on your own body by picking or shaving. What is the difference between a corn and a plantar wart? A corn is thickened skin from pressure. A plantar wart is caused by a virus and shows tiny black dots when the hard skin is pared down. Can I remove a wart myself? You can treat common warts and verrucas with pharmacy products, but never cut or burn them, and don’t treat warts on the face or genitals yourself. Does freezing warts hurt? It stings during the treatment and usually blisters afterwards. Several sessions may be needed. Are genital warts the same as ordinary warts? No. They are caused by different HPV types, are usually sexually transmitted, and need a doctor’s treatment.

title: Fever in children (demam budak): normal temperature, fever medicine, febrile seizures and when to see a doctor
desc: Fever is one of the most common reasons parents take a child to the clinic. What counts as a fever, how to take your child’s temperature, how to use paracetamol and ibuprofen safely, why dengue changes the advice in Malaysia, what to do in a febrile seizure, and the signs that need a doctor straight away.
headings: What is a normal temperature? (Suhu badan normal) · Caring for a child with a fever · Fever medicine (ubat demam budak) · When to see a doctor · Fever and dengue · Febrile seizures (sawan demam) · Common causes of fever in Malaysian children
keywords: Guides Fever in children Fever Demam Febrile seizure denggi aedes nyamuk mosquito payudara kanser cancer mammogram pink october vaksin suntikan jab immunisation kecemasan emergency a&e hospital klinik doctor doktor gp aesthetic estetik kecantikan beauty kulit skin botox filler laser facial
body: A temperature of 38°C or higher is a fever. Most fevers last 1 to 4 days. Any baby under 3 months with a temperature of 38°C or more, or 3 to 6 months with 39°C or more, needs to see a doctor urgently. Give paracetamol or ibuprofen if your child is distressed, not just to bring the number down. If dengue is possible, give paracetamol only, not ibuprofen. See a doctor if a fever lasts more than 2 to 3 days, as a blood test may be needed to check for dengue. Dengue warning signs often appear as the fever goes down. Febrile seizures (sawan demam) affect 3 to 4 in 100 young children. They are frightening but don’t cause brain damage. Lay the child on their side and call 999 if it lasts more than 5 minutes. Temperature What it means Up to about 37.4°C Normal 37.5–37.9°C Slightly raised (low-grade) 38°C or higher Fever How to measure: Use a digital thermometer . Feeling the forehead with your hand isn’t reliable. Don’t use mercury thermometers. For young children, put the thermometer in the armpit , with the arm held against the body, until it beeps. Armpit readings are slightly lower than true body temperature. Ear thermometers can be used from 6 months, and under-the-tongue readings from about 4 years. Forehead (infrared) thermometers are convenient but can give false readings, for example if the child has been in the sun or a hot room. Wait a few minutes after a bath or after taking off a blanket before measuring. Give plenty of fluids , little and often: water, milk, or oral rehydration salts. Keep breastfeeding. Dress your child in light clothing and use a light sheet. Don’t over-wrap them or bundle them in blankets. Don’t sponge your child with cold or ice water, or give cold baths. It makes them uncomfortable and doesn’t help. Let them rest, and offer food if they want it. There is no need to “starve a fever”. Check on them regularly, including during the night. Keep them home from school or nursery until they have had no fever for 24 hours without fever medicine. Fever itself isn’t harmful. Medicine is to make a distressed child more comfortable. If your child is playing and drinking, they may not need it. Paracetamol Ibuprofen Usual dose 15 mg per kg of body weight 5 to 10 mg per kg of body weight How often Every 4 to 6 hours, no more than 4 doses in 24 hours Every 6 to 8 hours, with food or milk Age From 2 months. Ask a doctor first for younger babies From 3 months and over 5 kg Avoid if — Possible dengue , chickenpox, dehydration, or asthma (unless a doctor advises) Dose by your child’s weight , not just age, and use the measuring syringe or cup that comes with the medicine. Check the strength on the label, as children’s syrups come in different strengths. In Malaysia, dengue is a real possibility with any fever. Ibuprofen and aspirin can raise the risk of bleeding in dengue, so use paracetamol unless a doctor has ruled dengue out. Don’t routinely alternate paracetamol and ibuprofen unless a doctor advises it. Never give aspirin to children under 16. Call 999 or go to an emergency department if your child: has a rash that doesn’t fade when you press a glass against it has a stiff neck, or is bothered by bright light is floppy, very drowsy or hard to wake is struggling to breathe, breathing very fast, or the chest sucks in with each breath has blue, grey, pale or blotchy skin or lips, or cold hands and feet has a fit (seizure) for the first time See a doctor the same day if: your baby is under 3 months with 38°C or more , or 3 to 6 months with 39°C or more your child shows signs of dehydration : fewer wet nappies, dry mouth, sunken eyes, no tears they can’t keep fluids down, or aren’t feeding the fever has lasted more than 2 to 3 days , or 5 days or more at any time you are worried, or your child seems to be getting worse Dengue usually causes a high fever for 3 to 5 days. The dangerous stage often starts as the fever goes down , when a falling temperature can give false reassurance. Watch for: tummy pain, or vomiting 3 or more times a day bleeding from the gums or nose, or blood in vomit or stools being restless, very tired or drowsy cold, clammy skin, or passing little urine Any of these needs a hospital straight away. If your child has had a fever for 2 to 3 days, see a doctor, who may arrange a blood test. See our guide to dengue in the first three days . A febrile seizure is a fit triggered by a fever. It affects 3 to 4 in 100 children, usually between 6 months and 5 years old. The child may stiffen, twitch or jerk, roll their eyes and become unresponsive, usually for less than 5 minutes. What to do: Stay calm and note the time . Lay your child on their side on a safe surface, away from anything hard or sharp. Don’t put anything in their mouth , and don’t try to hold them down. Don’t try to cool them by sponging or undressing them during the seizure. Call 999 if it is your child’s first seizure, it lasts more than 5 minutes, it affects only one side of the body, there is more than one seizure in 24 hours, or your child is still very drowsy an hour later. The good news: febrile seizures don’t cause brain damage, and very few children go on to have epilepsy. About 3 in 10 have another one with a later fever. Fever medicines don’t prevent febrile seizures, so there is no need to wake your child to give doses. Most fevers in children are caused by viruses and settle within a few days. colds, flu and other viral infections. See our guides to influenza and RSV . hand, foot and mouth disease and chickenpox tonsillitis and ear infections dengue urinary tract infections , which in babies may cause only fever and irritability vaccinations: a mild fever within a day or two of a vaccine is common and usually settles within 1 to 2 days. A fever 1 to 2 weeks after the MMR or chickenpox vaccine can also happen. See our vaccination schedule guide . For help deciding where to go, see our guide on clinic or emergency department . What temperature is a fever in a child? 38°C or higher. Up to about 37.4°C is normal, and 37.5 to 37.9°C is slightly raised. When should I take my child to the doctor for a fever? Straight away for a baby under 3 months with 38°C or more, or any danger signs such as a rash that doesn’t fade, breathing difficulty or drowsiness. Otherwise, if the fever lasts more than 2 to 3 days, or your child is dehydrated or getting worse. How much paracetamol can I give my child? Usually 15 mg per kg of body weight every 4 to 6 hours, with no more than 4 doses in 24 hours. Check the strength on the label and use the measuring device provided. Can I give ibuprofen for fever in Malaysia? Only from 3 months, and not if dengue is possible, as it can raise the risk of bleeding. Use paracetamol unless a doctor has ruled out dengue. Should I sponge my child with cold water? No. Cold sponging or ice baths make children uncomfortable and don’t help. Dress them lightly and give plenty of fluids. What should I do if my child has a febrile seizure? Note the time, lay them on their side somewhere safe, don’t put anything in their mouth, and call 999 if it is the first one or lasts more than 5 minutes. Do febrile seizures cause brain damage? No. They are frightening, but they don’t cause brain damage, and very few children go on to have epilepsy. When can my child go back to school after a fever? When they have had no fever for 24 hours without fever medicine and are feeling better.

title: Conjunctivitis and red eyes (sakit mata, mata merah): causes, treatment, how long it’s contagious, and emergencies
desc: Red, gritty, sticky eyes are usually conjunctivitis, which mostly clears on its own. How to tell viral, bacterial and allergic conjunctivitis apart, what helps, how to stop it spreading at home and school, and the red-eye symptoms that need an eye doctor the same day.
headings: Types of conjunctivitis · Treatment (ubat sakit mata) · Stopping it spreading · When a red eye is an emergency
keywords: Prevention Conjunctivitis (sakit mata) Conjunctivitis Sakit mata Red eye jerebu api ipu air pollutant index smoke payudara kanser cancer mammogram pink october kecemasan emergency a&e hospital klinik doctor doktor gp
body: Viral conjunctivitis is the most common type. It causes watery, red eyes, often with a cold, and usually clears in 1 to 2 weeks without treatment. Bacterial conjunctivitis causes thick yellow or green sticky discharge. It often clears in a few days, and antibiotic drops help it clear a little faster. Allergic conjunctivitis causes intense itching in both eyes. It isn’t contagious, and haze can trigger it: during the October 2026 haze, conjunctivitis cases at sentinel clinics rose by about a quarter in a week. Wash your hands often, don’t share towels or pillows, and stop wearing contact lenses until your eyes are better. See an eye doctor or go to an emergency department for eye pain, blurred vision, sensitivity to light, a chemical splash, an injury, or a red eye while wearing contact lenses. Type Typical signs Contagious? Viral Red, watery eyes, gritty feeling, often starts in one eye and spreads to the other, often with a cold or sore throat Yes, very Bacterial Red eye with thick yellow or green discharge, eyelids stuck together in the morning Yes Allergic Intense itching, watering and puffy eyelids, usually both eyes, often with sneezing No Irritant Redness and watering after smoke, haze, dust, chlorine or chemicals No Acute haemorrhagic conjunctivitis is a viral type that causes outbreaks in tropical countries, with bright red patches of blood on the white of the eye. A large outbreak in Melaka in 2002 to 2003 affected more than 10,000 people. In 2022, an outbreak in schools in Sri Aman, Sarawak affected 228 students. Haze is a common trigger of allergic and irritant conjunctivitis and dry eyes in Malaysia. See our guide to protecting your family during haze . For all types: Clean away discharge with cotton wool soaked in cooled boiled water, wiping from the inner to the outer corner, using a fresh piece for each eye. A cool, damp cloth over closed eyes soothes them. Lubricating eye drops (artificial tears) from a pharmacy ease grittiness. Don’t wear contact lenses until your eyes are back to normal. Throw away disposable lenses and cases you used while infected. Don’t wear eye make-up, and throw away eye make-up and drops you used since it started. Viral: there is no specific treatment and antibiotics don’t help. It usually clears in 1 to 2 weeks, sometimes longer. Bacterial: mild cases often clear in 2 to 5 days on their own. A Cochrane review found antibiotic eye drops modestly improve the chance of clearing quickly. In Malaysian government clinics the usual first choice is chloramphenicol drops. Allergic: avoid triggers where you can, rinse your eyes, and use antihistamine eye drops or tablets from a pharmacy. Avoid steroid eye drops unless an eye doctor prescribes them. Used wrongly, they can cause glaucoma and cataracts and make some infections, such as herpes, much worse. Don’t put breast milk, herbs or other home remedies in the eyes. Viral conjunctivitis often comes with a cold or sore throat. Wash your hands with soap for at least 20 seconds, especially after touching your eyes or putting in drops. Don’t rub your eyes. Don’t share towels, pillows, face cloths, eye make-up or eye drops. Wash pillowcases and towels in hot water. Avoid swimming pools until your eyes are better. School and work: advice varies. UK health guidance says there is no need to stay off for conjunctivitis unless you feel unwell, while US advice is to stay home while the eyes are red and discharging if you can’t avoid close contact. Malaysian schools and workplaces may have their own rules, especially during outbreaks, so check with them. Viral conjunctivitis spreads easily while the eyes are red and watery. Go to an emergency department or see an eye doctor the same day if you have: eye pain , rather than just grittiness or itch blurred or reduced vision that doesn’t clear with blinking pain when looking at bright light a very red eye with a severe headache, nausea or vomiting, or rainbow-coloured haloes around lights. These can be signs of acute glaucoma, which can quickly damage sight. a red, painful eye while wearing contact lenses . Take the lenses out. It can be a serious corneal infection (keratitis). an eye injury, or something stuck in the eye blisters or a cold sore near the eye a newborn baby (under 4 weeks) with red, sticky eyes Chemical in the eye: rinse it straight away with lots of clean running water for at least 20 minutes, keep rinsing on the way, and go to an emergency department. See our guide on clinic or emergency department . See a GP if conjunctivitis hasn’t improved after a week or two, keeps coming back, or you are unsure what is causing it. For a sore lump on the eyelid, see our guide to styes . What is sakit mata in English? Sakit mata or mata merah usually means conjunctivitis, also called pink eye: inflammation of the thin layer covering the white of the eye. How long is conjunctivitis contagious? Viral and bacterial conjunctivitis can spread while the eyes are red and discharging. Viral conjunctivitis usually lasts 1 to 2 weeks. Do I need antibiotic eye drops? Not for viral or allergic conjunctivitis. For bacterial conjunctivitis, drops help it clear a little faster, but many cases clear on their own within a few days. How do I know if conjunctivitis is viral or bacterial? Viral usually causes watery eyes, often with a cold. Bacterial causes thick yellow or green discharge that sticks the eyelids together. Allergic causes intense itching in both eyes. Can haze cause red eyes? Yes. Haze can trigger allergic and irritant conjunctivitis and dry eyes. Limit time outdoors and use lubricating drops. When is a red eye an emergency? With eye pain, blurred vision, sensitivity to light, a severe headache with vomiting, an injury or chemical splash, or a painful red eye while wearing contact lenses. Can I wear contact lenses with conjunctivitis? No. Stop wearing them until your eyes are back to normal, and throw away disposable lenses and cases you used while infected. Should my child stay home from school with conjunctivitis? Advice differs between countries, and Malaysian schools may have their own rules, especially during outbreaks. Check with the school, and keep the child home if they feel unwell.

title: PCOS (PMOS) in Malaysia: symptoms, diagnosis, treatment and fertility
desc: About 1 in 10 women has PCOS, and most don’t know it. What the symptoms are, how it is diagnosed, why it raises the risk of diabetes, the treatments that help with periods, acne, unwanted hair and weight, and the fertility options in Malaysia.
headings: What is PCOS? (PCOS maksud) · PCOS symptoms (simptom PCOS) · How PCOS is diagnosed · Long-term health risks and check-ups · PCOS treatment · PCOS and getting pregnant
keywords: Women's health PCOS (PMOS) Polycystic ovary syndrome PMOS Infertility kencing manis gula hba1c darah tinggi hypertension bp tekanan darah kesihatan mental depression anxiety stress kemurungan mengandung hamil pregnancy antenatal aesthetic estetik kecantikan beauty kulit skin botox filler laser facial
body: PCOS affects about 10 to 13% of women of reproductive age, and up to 7 in 10 don’t know they have it. Studies in the Klang Valley suggest similar rates in Malaysia. It is diagnosed when a woman has 2 of 3 features: irregular or absent periods, signs of high male hormones (such as excess hair or acne), and polycystic ovaries on ultrasound or a high AMH blood test. Despite the name, you don’t need cysts to have PCOS. In May 2026 an international consensus renamed it PMOS. PCOS raises the risk of type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, gestational diabetes and depression, so regular checks matter. Healthy eating, activity and modest weight loss help most women. The pill, metformin and other treatments manage symptoms, and letrozole is the first-choice medicine to help ovulation. PCOS is a long-term hormonal condition in which the ovaries make more androgens (male-type hormones) than usual and often don’t release an egg each month. Insulin resistance, where the body needs more insulin to keep blood sugar normal, plays a big part, which is why PCOS is linked to weight gain and diabetes. The World Health Organization estimates it affects 10 to 13% of women of reproductive age , and that up to 70% of them are undiagnosed. A 2021 survey in the Klang Valley found 10.5% of women reported having been diagnosed, and nearly half had poor knowledge of the condition. The ovaries of women with PCOS often have many small follicles, partly developed eggs, which look like “cysts” on a scan. These aren’t true cysts, and some women with PCOS don’t have them. In May 2026 , a global consensus published in The Lancet renamed the condition polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS) , or sindrom ovari metabolik poliendokrin in Malay. The new name is being phased in over several years, so you will see both. PCOS runs in families, and the cause isn’t fully understood. It isn’t caused by anything you did. irregular, infrequent or absent periods : cycles shorter than 21 days or longer than 35 days, or fewer than 8 periods a year excess hair on the face, chest, tummy or back (hirsutism) acne and oily skin, often along the jawline. See our guide to acne . thinning hair on the scalp weight gain, especially around the waist, and difficulty losing weight dark, velvety skin in the neck folds or armpits (acanthosis nigricans), a sign of insulin resistance difficulty getting pregnant low mood, anxiety and tiredness Symptoms vary a lot. Some women have only irregular periods; others have regular periods but troublesome acne or hair growth. Malaysian doctors report that diagnosis often comes 3 to 5 years after symptoms start, so it is worth seeing a doctor early. Under the 2023 International Evidence-based Guideline for PCOS, adults are diagnosed when they have at least 2 of these 3 , after other causes have been ruled out: Irregular or absent ovulation , shown by irregular periods High androgens : symptoms such as excess hair or acne, or high testosterone on a blood test Polycystic ovaries on an ultrasound scan (20 or more follicles in an ovary), or a high AMH blood test as an alternative If you have both irregular periods and high androgens, you don’t need a scan or AMH test. Teenagers need both irregular periods and high androgens. Ultrasound and AMH aren’t used to diagnose PCOS within 8 years of the first period, as many young women naturally have polycystic-looking ovaries. Blood tests usually include testosterone, and tests to rule out other causes, such as thyroid (TSH), prolactin and other hormones. If you are on the pill, it may affect the results. A GP can start these tests and refer you to a gynaecologist or endocrinologist if needed. See our guide to thyroid problems , which can also cause irregular periods. PCOS is a lifelong condition, and it affects more than the ovaries. Women with PCOS have a higher risk of: type 2 diabetes and gestational diabetes in pregnancy high blood pressure and high cholesterol fatty liver and sleep apnoea thickening of the womb lining, and endometrial cancer, if periods are very infrequent anxiety, depression and eating problems Recommended checks: blood sugar at diagnosis, then every 1 to 3 years. An oral glucose tolerance test is the most accurate. See our guide to normal blood sugar levels . cholesterol at diagnosis blood pressure every year a check on your mood and wellbeing Asian women tend to develop diabetes at a lower weight, so even women with PCOS at a “normal” weight should have their blood sugar checked. Malaysia uses lower BMI cut-offs: see our BMI calculator . There is no cure, but symptoms and risks can be well managed. Treatment depends on what bothers you most and whether you want to get pregnant. Lifestyle first Healthy eating and regular activity help everyone with PCOS. No single diet is best, so choose one you can keep to: fewer sugary drinks and refined carbohydrates, more vegetables, wholegrains and protein. Aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week. If you are overweight, even modest weight loss can bring back regular periods and ovulation. In a 2026 analysis, more than half of women with PCOS who lost weight started ovulating again. A waist of 80 cm or less is a useful target. Medicines Treatment Used for Combined contraceptive pill Regular periods, less acne and hair growth, and protecting the womb lining Progestogen tablets or a hormonal coil Protecting the womb lining if you have few periods and can’t take the pill Metformin Insulin resistance, weight and blood sugar, especially with a higher BMI Anti-androgen medicines Excess hair or hair loss, after at least 6 months on the pill, with reliable contraception Laser hair removal, creams Facial and body hair, acne Weight-loss medicines (such as GLP-1 injections) Weight, when lifestyle changes aren’t enough. Not for use when trying to conceive or in pregnancy. See our guide to weight-loss injections Supplements: inositol is widely marketed for PCOS. The international guideline says it may be considered, but the evidence of benefit is limited, and its use for fertility is experimental. Talk to your doctor before spending on supplements. Healthy eating and activity are the first step in managing PCOS, whatever your weight. Many women with PCOS get pregnant naturally or with simple treatment. If you aren’t ovulating regularly: Letrozole tablets are the first-choice medicine to help you ovulate, ahead of clomiphene. If that doesn’t work, options include hormone injections (gonadotrophins) with close ultrasound monitoring, or a keyhole operation on the ovaries. IVF is used if other treatments haven’t worked or there are other fertility problems. See a doctor if you have been trying for 12 months, or 6 months if you are 35 or over, or sooner if your periods are very irregular. Fertility help in Malaysia: Government hospitals offer ovulation treatment and IVF, although waiting times can be long. Under LPPKN’s BuAI programme , eligible couples can receive up to 2 cycles of IUI (intrauterine insemination) treatment. Priority goes to lower-income households, and couples need to meet age and income conditions. You can withdraw from EPF Account 2 for fertility treatment, and claim tax relief for it. During pregnancy, women with PCOS have a higher risk of gestational diabetes and high blood pressure, so they should be screened early. See our pregnancy week-by-week guide . What is PCOS? Polycystic ovary syndrome, a common hormone condition that causes irregular periods, high male-type hormones and often polycystic-looking ovaries. In 2026 it was renamed PMOS. What are the first signs of PCOS? Usually irregular or missed periods, often with acne, excess facial or body hair, weight gain or thinning scalp hair. Can I have PCOS without cysts? Yes. You only need 2 of the 3 features to be diagnosed, so many women with PCOS have normal-looking ovaries on a scan. Can PCOS be cured? There is no cure, but symptoms can be well controlled with lifestyle changes and treatment, and many women find symptoms ease with time. Can I get pregnant with PCOS? Yes. Many women with PCOS conceive naturally or with treatment. Letrozole is the first-choice medicine to help ovulation. Does PCOS cause weight gain? PCOS makes weight gain easier and weight loss harder because of insulin resistance. Even modest weight loss can improve periods and fertility. Do inositol supplements work for PCOS? The international guideline says the evidence of benefit is limited. They may be considered, but talk to your doctor first. What does PMOS mean? Polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, the new name for PCOS agreed in 2026, which reflects that the condition affects hormones and metabolism, not just the ovaries.

title: Pneumonia in Malaysia: symptoms, walking pneumonia, when to go to hospital, and the pneumococcal vaccine
desc: Pneumonia is one of the top two causes of death in Malaysia, and the leading one among people aged 60 and over. The symptoms in adults, older people and children, what walking pneumonia is, the danger signs that need a hospital, and who should get the pneumococcal vaccine.
headings: Pneumonia in Malaysia · What causes pneumonia? · Symptoms of pneumonia · When to see a doctor or go to hospital · Treatment and recovery · The pneumococcal vaccine · Other ways to lower your risk
keywords: Prevention Pneumonia and the pneumococcal vaccine Pneumonia Pneumococcal vaccine Radang paru-paru kencing manis gula hba1c darah tinggi hypertension bp tekanan darah vaksin suntikan jab immunisation kecemasan emergency a&e hospital klinik doctor doktor gp aesthetic estetik kecantikan beauty kulit skin botox filler laser facial
body: Pneumonia was the 2nd leading cause of medically certified deaths in Malaysia in 2024, with 15,332 deaths, and the leading cause among people aged 60 and over. Typical symptoms are cough with phlegm, fever, fast or difficult breathing and chest pain on breathing. Older people may simply become confused. Go to an emergency department for severe breathlessness, blue or grey lips, confusion, coughing up blood, or a baby who is floppy or breathing fast with the chest sucking in. Bacterial pneumonia is treated with antibiotics. Most people recover in 2 to 4 weeks, but the cough and tiredness can last longer. Babies get the pneumococcal vaccine free under the National Immunisation Programme. Older adults and people with long-term conditions can get it at private clinics. According to the Department of Statistics Malaysia, pneumonia caused 15,332 deaths in 2024 , 11.5% of medically certified deaths. It was the leading cause of death in 2023, and in 2024 was second only to heart disease. It remained the leading cause of death among people aged 60 and over , among women, and among children aged 14 and under. Respiratory infections rise at the end of each year and around the festive seasons, when people travel and gather, which is why vaccination before then matters. Bacteria: Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus) is the most common bacterial cause. Viruses: including flu, RSV and COVID-19. Viral pneumonia can be followed by a bacterial infection. Mycoplasma pneumoniae : causes “walking pneumonia”, especially in children and young adults. People at higher risk include babies and young children, adults over 65, smokers, and people with diabetes, heart, lung (including asthma and COPD), kidney or liver disease, or a weak immune system. In adults: a cough, often with yellow, green or bloodstained phlegm fever, sweating and shivering fast breathing or feeling breathless, even at rest sharp chest pain that is worse when you breathe in or cough tiredness and loss of appetite In older people , pneumonia may show up as sudden confusion , falls or not eating, with fewer chest symptoms. In babies and young children , the key signs are fast breathing and the lower chest sucking in with each breath, along with fever, cough, poor feeding and being unusually sleepy. Walking pneumonia is an informal name for a milder pneumonia, usually caused by Mycoplasma , where people often stay up and about. Symptoms start 1 to 4 weeks after exposure, and the cough builds slowly and can last for weeks. It still needs a doctor, as some strains don’t respond to common antibiotics. In 2025, doctors in Kelantan described a group of children who needed oxygen for Mycoplasma pneumonia. Call 999 or go to an emergency department if: you are struggling to breathe or can’t finish a sentence your lips, tongue or skin look blue, grey or very pale you are coughing up blood someone becomes confused, very drowsy or hard to wake a baby or child is breathing fast with the chest sucking in, can’t drink or feed, has a fit, or is floppy See a doctor the same day for a cough with fever and breathlessness, chest pain on breathing, or a cough that has lasted 3 weeks or is getting worse. The doctor will listen to your chest and check your oxygen level with a finger clip (pulse oximeter), and may arrange a chest X-ray and blood tests. Malaysian doctors use a simple score called CURB-65, based on confusion, kidney blood test, breathing rate, blood pressure and age 65 or over, to decide who can be treated at home and who needs hospital. See our guide on clinic or emergency department . Bacterial pneumonia is treated with antibiotics. Take the full course as prescribed. Viral pneumonia doesn’t respond to antibiotics, although flu may be treated with antiviral medicine if started early. See our guide to influenza A . At home: rest, drink plenty of fluids, and use paracetamol for fever and pain. Avoid cough suppressants, which stop you clearing phlegm. Don’t smoke. Go back to the doctor if you aren’t improving after 2 to 3 days of treatment, or you get worse at any time. Most people feel better within 2 to 4 weeks, but the cough and tiredness can take longer, especially in older people. For a cough that lingers, see our guide to a cough that won’t go away . A doctor can check your oxygen level and chest, and decide whether you can be treated at home. Pneumococcal vaccines protect against the bacterium that causes most bacterial pneumonia, as well as meningitis and blood infections. There are two main kinds: conjugate vaccines (PCV), which come in versions covering 10 to 21 types of pneumococcus, and a polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23). Babies: the pneumococcal conjugate vaccine has been part of Malaysia’s National Immunisation Programme since December 2020, for babies born from 2020. It is given at 4 and 6 months, with a booster at 15 months , free at government clinics. See our baby vaccination schedule . Adults: there is no free national programme for adults, and the vaccine is mainly available at private clinics . Malaysian recommendations for older adults, published in 2025, advise: a single dose of a broad conjugate vaccine (PCV20), or a conjugate vaccine followed by PPSV23 a year later Who should consider it: adults aged 60 and over . The US now recommends it from 50. younger adults with diabetes , chronic heart, lung (including asthma and COPD), kidney or liver disease, smokers, people with heavy alcohol use, and people with a weak immune system or no working spleen people going on Hajj or Umrah , where respiratory infections spread easily Only about 3 in 10 older people in a 2025 Klang Valley study had been vaccinated. Ask your GP which vaccine and schedule suit you, as this depends on your age, health and any previous doses. Side effects are usually mild: a sore, red or swollen arm, fever, tiredness, headache or aches for a day or two. It can be given at the same visit as the flu vaccine. Get a yearly flu vaccine , especially if you are 60 or over or have a long-term condition. Older adults can also ask about the RSV vaccine and COVID-19 boosters. Stop smoking and vaping. Smoking damages the lungs’ defences. Wash your hands, cover coughs and sneezes, and wear a mask if you have a respiratory infection and must be around older or vulnerable people. Keep diabetes and other long-term conditions well controlled. What are the first signs of pneumonia? Usually a cough with phlegm, fever, and breathing that is faster or more difficult than normal, sometimes with chest pain when breathing in. Older people may become confused. What is walking pneumonia? An informal name for milder pneumonia, usually caused by Mycoplasma, where people stay up and about. The cough builds slowly and can last for weeks. It still needs a doctor. Is pneumonia contagious? The germs that cause it, such as pneumococcus, flu and Mycoplasma, spread through coughs and sneezes, although not everyone who catches them develops pneumonia. How long does pneumonia take to recover from? Most people feel better in 2 to 4 weeks, but the cough and tiredness can last longer, especially in older people. Who should get the pneumococcal vaccine? Babies under the National Immunisation Programme, adults aged 60 and over, and younger adults with diabetes, heart, lung, kidney or liver disease, smokers and people with a weak immune system. Is the pneumococcal vaccine free for adults in Malaysia? There is no national programme for adults, so it is mainly given at private clinics. Babies get it free under the National Immunisation Programme. Do adults need more than one pneumococcal vaccine? It depends on the vaccine. A single dose of a broad conjugate vaccine may be enough, or a conjugate vaccine may be followed by a second type a year later. Ask your doctor. Can I get the pneumococcal and flu vaccines together? Yes, they can be given at the same visit.

title: Food poisoning and gastroenteritis (keracunan makanan, cirit-birit): symptoms, rehydration and when to see a doctor
desc: Vomiting and diarrhoea after a meal, a kenduri or a school event? Most food poisoning and stomach bugs settle within a few days with fluids. The common causes, how to rehydrate properly, which medicines are safe, the danger signs that need a doctor, and how to keep food safe in Malaysia’s heat.
headings: Food poisoning in Malaysia · Common causes, and how soon symptoms start · Symptoms and how long they last · Rehydration: the most important treatment · Medicines: what helps and what to avoid · When to see a doctor · Preventing food poisoning
keywords: Prevention Food poisoning and gastroenteritis Food poisoning Gastroenteritis Keracunan makanan kencing manis gula hba1c payudara kanser cancer mammogram pink october mengandung hamil pregnancy antenatal vaksin suntikan jab immunisation kecemasan emergency a&e hospital klinik doctor doktor gp
body: Malaysia records thousands of food poisoning cases every year, often in outbreaks linked to schools, caterers and events. Symptoms can start within an hour or two of eating (toxins in food such as rice or pastries left out) or up to several days later (bacteria such as Salmonella). Most cases settle within a few days. Vomiting usually stops within 1 to 2 days and diarrhoea within 5 to 7 days. Oral rehydration salts (ORS) are the best way to replace lost fluid. Avoid fizzy drinks and fruit juice. Keep breastfeeding babies. See a doctor for blood in the stool, high fever, signs of dehydration, vomiting that stops you keeping fluids down, diarrhoea lasting more than 3 days, or if a baby, older person or pregnant woman is unwell. Food poisoning is a notifiable disease in Malaysia, so doctors must report cases to the Ministry of Health. The national rate rose from 18.4 per 100,000 people in 2021 to 51 per 100,000 in 2023 . Cases then fell: from January to early September 2025 there were 12,821 cases, against 18,034 in the same period of 2024. The ministry aims to keep the rate below 50 per 100,000 by 2030. Outbreaks are most often linked to food prepared in bulk, such as at schools and hostels, caterers and events: In September 2026, about 160 students and staff at a boarding school in Lenggong, Perak fell ill after a school programme. The caterer was ordered to close. In July 2025, 427 college students in Kota Bharu fell ill, and an unlicensed home caterer was shut down. If several people fall ill after the same meal, tell the clinic, so the health office can investigate.
