title: Hepatitis B in Malaysia: symptoms, test results, the adult vaccine and living with it
desc: About 1 million Malaysians live with hepatitis B, and most don’t know it. How it spreads and doesn’t, what your blood test results mean, who should get the adult vaccine, what it means for work, and how chronic hepatitis B is monitored and treated.
headings: What is hepatitis B? (Apa itu hepatitis B) · How hepatitis B spreads, and how it doesn’t · Symptoms of hepatitis B · Hepatitis B tests: what your results mean · The hepatitis B vaccine · Hepatitis B, FOMEMA and work · Living with chronic hepatitis B
keywords: Prevention Hepatitis B Hepatitis B Hepatitis B vaccine HBsAg kencing manis gula hba1c payudara kanser cancer mammogram pink october mengandung hamil pregnancy antenatal vaksin suntikan jab immunisation klinik doctor doktor gp aesthetic estetik kecantikan beauty kulit skin botox filler laser facial
body: About 1 million Malaysians are estimated to live with chronic hepatitis B. In one community study, only about 1 in 8 knew they had it. It spreads through blood and body fluids: from mother to baby at birth, through sex, and through shared needles, razors or toothbrushes. It doesn’t spread through sharing food, utensils, hugging or coughing. The HBsAg test shows whether you have the virus now. The anti-HBs test shows whether you are protected. Babies in Malaysia have been vaccinated since 1989. Adults who aren’t immune can have 3 doses, usually at 0, 1 and 6 months, at a GP clinic. People with chronic hepatitis B need check-ups every 6 to 12 months. Antiviral tablets, when needed, greatly lower the risk of cirrhosis and liver cancer. Hepatitis B is a liver infection caused by the hepatitis B virus (HBV). It can be: acute: a new infection in the first 6 months. Most healthy adults clear the virus within a few months. chronic: when the virus stays for more than 6 months. This happens to about 9 in 10 babies infected at birth, about 3 in 10 young children, but fewer than 1 in 20 adults . Over decades, chronic hepatitis B can scar the liver ( cirrhosis ) and cause liver cancer . Hepatitis B is the leading cause of liver cancer in Malaysia. In Malaysia: before vaccination began in 1989, about 5 to 7% of people carried the virus. Rates are now much lower among those born after 1989. Even so, an estimated 1 million people live with chronic hepatitis B. Notified cases rose from 3,781 in 2021 to 8,138 in 2025, partly because more people are being tested, and Malaysia aims to eliminate hepatitis B as a public health threat by 2030. Can spread through Doesn’t spread through Mother to baby at birth Sharing food, drinks or utensils Sex without a condom Hugging, kissing or holding hands Sharing needles or drug equipment Coughing or sneezing Sharing razors, toothbrushes or nail clippers Breastfeeding Unsterile tattoo, piercing or medical equipment Food or water So people with hepatitis B can work, eat with family and friends, and live normally. Household members and sexual partners should be tested and vaccinated. Many people, especially children, have no symptoms . When symptoms of a new infection occur, they usually start about 3 months after exposure: yellowing of the skin and eyes ( jaundice ) dark urine and pale stools tiredness, fever, loss of appetite, nausea and vomiting pain in the upper right tummy, and joint pain Chronic hepatitis B is usually silent for years, which is why testing matters. See a doctor promptly if you develop jaundice. The main blood tests are: HBsAg (hepatitis B surface antigen): positive means you have the virus now. Anti-HBs (surface antibody): positive means you are protected, from vaccination or past infection. A level of 10 mIU/mL or more counts as protected. Anti-HBc (core antibody): positive means you have been infected at some time. HBsAg Anti-HBc Anti-HBs What it usually means Negative Negative Negative Not immune : get vaccinated Negative Negative Positive Protected by vaccination Negative Positive Positive Past infection, now cleared , and protected Positive Positive Negative Current infection : acute or chronic, depending on further tests If you have hepatitis B, your doctor will also check your liver function (ALT), the amount of virus ( HBV DNA ), and HBeAg, and may arrange an ultrasound or a FibroScan to check for liver scarring. Other combinations, such as anti-HBc positive on its own, need a doctor to interpret. In pregnancy: antenatal clinics in Malaysia screen pregnant women for hepatitis B. Babies of mothers with hepatitis B are given the vaccine and an immunoglobulin injection soon after birth, and some mothers are given antiviral tablets late in pregnancy, which together prevent most infections in babies. Children: under the National Immunisation Programme, babies get a hepatitis B dose within 24 hours of birth, then the 6-in-1 vaccine at 2, 3 and 5 months with a booster at 18 months. In December 2025 the Ministry of Health confirmed it would keep the universal birth dose. See our baby vaccination schedule . Adults: if you were born before 1989 or aren’t sure you were vaccinated, ask for a blood test. If you aren’t immune, the usual adult course is: 3 doses , at 0, 1 and 6 months faster schedules are available, for example before travel or work, with an extra dose at 12 months a combined hepatitis A and B vaccine is also available, usually given at 0, 1 and 6 months Especially recommended for: partners and household members of someone with hepatitis B healthcare workers, carers and others who may come into contact with blood people with chronic liver disease, kidney disease or on dialysis, diabetes, HIV or hepatitis C people who have several sexual partners or an STI, and people who inject drugs travellers and people moving to areas where hepatitis B is common Protection lasts at least 20 years and probably for life, so healthy people don’t need routine boosters. Healthcare workers and others at ongoing risk usually have an anti-HBs test 1 to 2 months after the last dose to confirm they responded. If not, a second course is given. Side effects are usually just a sore arm and, sometimes, a mild fever. The adult hepatitis B vaccine is usually 3 doses over 6 months. Foreign workers: hepatitis B is one of the conditions tested in the FOMEMA medical exam. A positive HBsAg result currently means the worker is classed as unsuitable for employment in Malaysia. FOMEMA recorded 3,347 hepatitis B cases among foreign workers in 2023. See our guide to the FOMEMA medical check-up . Malaysian workers: some employers, especially in healthcare, ask for a hepatitis B test or proof of vaccination. Having hepatitis B doesn’t stop you doing most jobs, and international guidance says healthcare workers with hepatitis B shouldn’t automatically be excluded from work. Food handlers need a typhoid injection rather than a hepatitis B test, as hepatitis B doesn’t spread through food. See our guide to the typhoid injection for food handlers . Regular check-ups: blood tests every 6 to 12 months, and for many people an ultrasound (often with an AFP blood test) every 6 months to look for early liver cancer. Treatment: not everyone needs medicine. If the virus is active or the liver is damaged, a specialist may start antiviral tablets such as tenofovir or entecavir, usually taken long term. They control the virus and greatly lower the risk of cirrhosis and liver cancer. They are available at government hospitals. Protect your liver: avoid alcohol, keep to a healthy weight, and check with your doctor before taking herbal remedies or new medicines. Protect others: make sure your partner and family are tested and vaccinated, use condoms with partners who aren’t immune, and don’t share razors or toothbrushes. Get vaccinated against hepatitis A if you aren’t immune, as a second infection can harm your liver. Malaysia’s hepatitis services are still reaching only a minority of people with the infection, partly because it causes no symptoms. If you have a family member with hepatitis B, or were born before 1989 and have never been tested, ask your doctor for a test. What is hepatitis B? A virus that infects the liver. Most adults clear it, but people infected as babies or young children often carry it for life, which can lead to cirrhosis and liver cancer. How do you get hepatitis B? Through blood and body fluids: from mother to baby at birth, through sex, and by sharing needles, razors or toothbrushes. Not through sharing food, utensils, hugging or coughing. What does a positive HBsAg mean? That you have the hepatitis B virus now. Further tests show whether the infection is new or chronic and whether you need treatment. How many doses of hepatitis B vaccine do adults need? Usually 3 doses, at 0, 1 and 6 months. Faster schedules are available, with an extra dose at 12 months. Do I need a hepatitis B booster? Healthy people who completed the course usually don’t. Healthcare workers and others at ongoing risk may have a blood test to check they responded. Is there a combined hepatitis A and B vaccine? Yes. It is usually given as 3 doses at 0, 1 and 6 months, and protects against both viruses. Can hepatitis B be cured? Chronic hepatitis B usually can’t be cured, but antiviral tablets control it well and greatly lower the risk of liver damage and cancer. Can a foreign worker with hepatitis B work in Malaysia? Under current FOMEMA rules, a worker who tests positive for hepatitis B is classed as unsuitable for employment.

title: Pap smear and HPV test in Malaysia: who needs one, how often, what to expect and free options
desc: Cervical cancer is one of the most common cancers in Malaysian women, and one of the most preventable. Who should have a Pap smear or HPV test and how often, what happens on the day, what your results mean, and where to get screened free.
headings: Why cervical screening matters · Who needs a Pap smear or HPV test, and how often? · Pap smear vs HPV test: what’s the difference? · What happens during a Pap smear · Understanding your results · Where to get a free or low-cost Pap smear or HPV test · The HPV vaccine and screening · Symptoms that need a doctor
keywords: Women's health Pap smear and HPV test Pap smear HPV test Cervical cancer screening payudara kanser cancer mammogram pink october mengandung hamil pregnancy antenatal vaksin suntikan jab immunisation klinik doctor doktor gp saringan check-up checkup medical
body: Cervical cancer is the 3rd most common cancer in Malaysian women, with about 2,000 new cases and nearly 1,000 deaths a year. Almost all cases are caused by the human papillomavirus (HPV). Ministry of Health guidance: sexually active women aged 20 to 65 should have a Pap smear yearly for 2 years, then every 3 years if the results are normal. The HPV DNA test is more sensitive. It is recommended from age 30, and if it is negative you usually don’t need another for 5 years. You can often take the sample yourself. Pap smears are free at government health clinics, and free HPV tests are available to eligible women through LPPKN and Program ROSE. Women who have had the HPV vaccine still need screening. Cervical cancer develops slowly. Long-lasting infection with high-risk types of HPV , a very common virus spread through sexual contact, can cause abnormal cells on the cervix. Over 10 to 15 years, some of these can turn into cancer. Screening finds the virus or the abnormal cells early, when simple treatment prevents cancer from developing. International estimates for 2024 put cervical cancer as the 3rd most common cancer in Malaysian women , with 1,968 new cases and 964 deaths. Screening coverage is improving but still low: the National Health and Morbidity Survey found that 43.2% of women aged 30 to 65 had been screened in 2023, up from 23.1% in 2019. Many cases in Malaysia are still found at a late stage, when treatment is harder. Test Who How often Pap smear Women aged 20 to 65 who have ever been sexually active Yearly for the first 2 years, then every 3 years if normal HPV DNA test Women aged 30 and over (MOH guidance: 30 to 49; LPPKN and Program ROSE offer it to 30 to 65) Every 5 years if negative Under the Ministry of Health’s HPV testing guideline, women aged 21 to 29 and 50 to 65 are still advised to have Pap smears. The ministry is gradually moving towards HPV testing as the main screening test, so ask the clinic which one suits you. You still need screening if you have had the HPV vaccine, are in a long-term relationship, or haven’t had sex for some years. If you have never had any sexual contact , your risk is very low. Discuss with your doctor whether you need screening. After a hysterectomy that removed the cervix for a non-cancer reason, you usually don’t need screening. Check with your doctor if you aren’t sure. Over 65 , you can usually stop if your recent results have been normal. If you are pregnant , tell the doctor or nurse. Routine screening is often postponed until after the birth. A Pap smear (cervical cytology) looks at cells from the cervix under a microscope for abnormal changes. Malaysia has mostly moved from the conventional smear on a glass slide to liquid-based cytology , where the sample is rinsed into a vial of liquid, which gives clearer results. An HPV DNA test looks for the high-risk HPV types that cause almost all cervical cancers. It picks up risk earlier than a Pap smear, so a negative result means you can safely wait 5 years. The sample can be taken by a doctor or nurse, or by you with a soft swab ( self-sampling ). If your HPV test is positive, the same sample or a new one is usually checked with cytology to decide the next step. You undress from the waist down and lie on the examination bed with your knees bent. You can ask for a female doctor or nurse, or for someone to be with you. The doctor or nurse gently inserts a speculum (sometimes called mulut itik , “duck’s beak”) into the vagina to see the cervix. A small soft brush is used to collect cells from the cervix. This takes a few seconds. The test itself takes less than 5 minutes , and the visit about 10 minutes. It can feel uncomfortable but shouldn’t be painful. Tell the doctor if it hurts. You can ask them to stop at any time, or to use a smaller speculum. Light spotting afterwards is normal. How to prepare: Book the test for a time when you aren’t having your period , ideally in the middle of your cycle. For 24 to 48 hours before, avoid sex, and don’t use vaginal creams, pessaries, lubricants or douches. Screening takes only a few minutes and can be done at government health clinics, LPPKN clinics and private clinics. Result What it means Usual next step Normal / HPV negative No abnormal cells or high-risk HPV found Routine screening (3 years for Pap, 5 years for HPV) Unsatisfactory The sample couldn’t be read Repeat the test, usually within 3 months ASC-US or LSIL Mild cell changes, usually caused by HPV and often clearing by themselves Repeat test, often in 1 year, or colposcopy ASC-H or HSIL More serious cell changes that could become cancer if untreated Colposcopy HPV 16 or 18 positive The two highest-risk HPV types Colposcopy Other high-risk HPV positive A high-risk type other than 16 or 18 Cytology on the sample, then a repeat test in 1 year or colposcopy An abnormal result doesn’t mean you have cancer . Most HPV infections clear within 1 to 2 years. A colposcopy is a closer look at the cervix with a magnifying instrument, done in a clinic. If abnormal cells are found, they can be removed with a quick procedure, such as LLETZ (LEEP), which usually prevents cancer. Government health clinics (Klinik Kesihatan): Pap smears have been free at government facilities since 1998, and some clinics offer HPV testing. LPPKN (Klinik Nur Sejahtera): free HPV DNA self-sampling tests for eligible women aged 30 to 65 at participating clinics, under a government subsidy. Program ROSE: HPV self-sampling for women aged 30 to 65, free or subsidised depending on nationality and income, with results sent to your phone. It runs with partner hospitals and clinics. PERKESO Health Screening Programme: eligible contributors aged 40 and over can have a Pap smear as part of the free screening. See our guide to free health screening in Malaysia . Private GP and women’s clinics: you can usually be seen quickly. In January 2026, The Star reported typical private prices of around RM40 for a Pap smear and around RM250 for an HPV DNA test. Prices vary, so ask when you book. Malaysia has vaccinated schoolgirls against HPV since 2010, with coverage above 90%. From 2026 the school programme moved from Form 1 to Year 6 girls. The vaccine prevents most, but not all, cancer-causing HPV infections, and it doesn’t clear an infection you already have. That is why vaccinated women still need screening. See our guide to the HPV vaccine in Malaysia . Screening is for women without symptoms. Don’t wait for your next test if you have: bleeding between periods, after sex, or after the menopause unusual or smelly vaginal discharge pain in the pelvis or during sex These are usually caused by something less serious, but they should be checked. Women should also be breast aware: see our guide to breast cancer screening . How often should I have a Pap smear in Malaysia? If you are 20 to 65 and have been sexually active, yearly for the first 2 years, then every 3 years if the results are normal. If you have an HPV test and it is negative, the next one is usually in 5 years. Is a Pap smear painful? It can be uncomfortable but shouldn’t be painful, and takes less than 5 minutes. Tell the doctor if it hurts. You can ask them to stop, or to use a smaller speculum. What is the difference between a Pap smear and an HPV test? A Pap smear looks for abnormal cells on the cervix. An HPV test looks for the high-risk virus that causes those changes, so it picks up risk earlier and is repeated less often. Where can I get a free Pap smear? At government health clinics. Eligible women aged 30 to 65 can also get a free HPV test through LPPKN or Program ROSE, and PERKESO contributors aged 40 and over can have a Pap smear in its free health screening. How much is a Pap smear at a private clinic? Prices vary. In January 2026 The Star reported around RM40 for a Pap smear and around RM250 for an HPV DNA test at private clinics. Can I have a Pap smear during my period? It is best to book for a time when you aren’t having your period, as blood can make the sample harder to read. Do I need a Pap smear if I’ve had the HPV vaccine? Yes. The vaccine doesn’t protect against every cancer-causing HPV type, so vaccinated women still need regular screening. Does an abnormal Pap smear mean cancer? No. Most abnormal results are mild changes caused by HPV that often clear on their own. Some need a closer look (colposcopy) and simple treatment to stop them turning into cancer.

title: Tetanus injection (ATT) in Malaysia: when you need one after a cut, rusty nail or bite
desc: Tetanus is rare in Malaysia but often fatal, and it can follow a small, dirty wound. When a cut, rusty nail, animal bite or burn needs a tetanus injection (ATT), how often adults need a booster, and what vaccines Malaysian children and pregnant women get.
headings: What is tetanus? · Symptoms of tetanus · Do I need a tetanus injection after a wound? · First aid for cuts and puncture wounds · Tetanus vaccines in Malaysia’s immunisation schedule · Tetanus boosters for adults · Tetanus vaccine in pregnancy · Side effects of the tetanus injection
keywords: Prevention Tetanus injection (ATT) Tetanus Tetanus toxoid Suntikan tetanus darah tinggi hypertension bp tekanan darah mengandung hamil pregnancy antenatal vaksin suntikan jab immunisation kecemasan emergency a&e hospital klinik doctor doktor gp aesthetic estetik kecantikan beauty kulit skin botox filler laser facial
body: Tetanus is caused by bacteria whose spores live in soil, dust, manure and on rusty or dirty objects. They enter through wounds and make a toxin that causes painful muscle spasms and lockjaw. After a clean, minor cut, you need a booster if your last tetanus dose was 10 or more years ago. After a dirty or deep wound, you need one if it was 5 or more years ago. If you have never been fully vaccinated, or don’t know, and the wound is dirty or deep, you may need tetanus immunoglobulin as well as the vaccine. Malaysian children get 6 tetanus doses: at 2, 3, 5 and 18 months, at 7 years and at 15 years. Adults should have a booster about every 10 years. Pregnant women get free tetanus-containing vaccines at government clinics, including Tdap, to protect themselves and the baby. Tetanus is caused by Clostridium tetani . Its spores are found everywhere in the environment, including soil, dust, ash and animal and human faeces , and on rusty or dirty objects such as nails, wire and tools. The rust itself doesn’t cause tetanus; it is the dirt on the object, and the deep puncture it makes, that matter. When spores get into a wound, especially a deep one with little air, they make a toxin that attacks the nerves. Tetanus doesn’t spread from person to person, and having it doesn’t make you immune , so people who recover still need vaccinating. Symptoms usually start 3 to 21 days after the injury, most often within 2 weeks, and the wound may already have healed: stiffness and cramping of the jaw ( lockjaw ), so you can’t open your mouth stiff neck, difficulty swallowing painful muscle stiffness and spasms that spread down the body, which can be set off by noise or touch fever, sweating, and changes in blood pressure and heart rate Tetanus is a medical emergency needing intensive care. Even with treatment, it can be fatal, especially in older people. In one case reported by Malaysian doctors in 2024, a 63-year-old man in Seremban who cut his knee after falling into a drain developed lockjaw 8 days later and died despite treatment. Call 999 or go to an emergency department if someone develops jaw stiffness, difficulty swallowing or muscle spasms after an injury. It depends on the type of wound and when you last had a tetanus vaccine: Your vaccination history Clean, minor wound Dirty, deep or tetanus-prone wound Fully vaccinated, last dose under 5 years ago No jab needed No jab needed Fully vaccinated, last dose 5 to 10 years ago No jab needed Booster Fully vaccinated, last dose 10 or more years ago Booster Booster Not fully vaccinated, or don’t know Vaccine , and complete the course Vaccine and tetanus immunoglobulin , and complete the course Tetanus-prone wounds include: puncture wounds, such as stepping on a nail or a gardening injury wounds contaminated with soil, manure, faeces or saliva, including animal and human bites wounds with something stuck in them, or with dead or crushed tissue burns, crush injuries and broken bones that pierce the skin wounds that weren’t cleaned for several hours Get the jab as soon as possible , ideally on the day. If you missed that, it is still worth getting later. Tetanus immunoglobulin is an injection of ready-made antibodies for high-risk cases, usually given in a hospital emergency department. Antibiotics don’t prevent tetanus. For dog and cat bites, a doctor will also check whether you need rabies vaccination. Wash your hands, then rinse the wound well under clean running water for several minutes and wash around it with soap. Remove visible dirt. Don’t dig deep for objects that are stuck in. Leave those for a doctor. Stop bleeding with firm pressure using a clean cloth, then cover with a clean dressing. See a doctor if the wound is deep, dirty, gaping, caused by a bite or a rusty or dirty object, or you aren’t sure when your last tetanus jab was. Go to an emergency department for deep or heavily contaminated wounds, bleeding that won’t stop, or wounds that may need stitches or cleaning under anaesthetic. Deep, dirty wounds need proper cleaning as well as the jab. See our guide on clinic or emergency department . During floods , the Ministry of Health advises people with open wounds not to wade, bathe or play in floodwater. Clean and cover any cuts quickly, and check your tetanus status. See our guide to floods and your health . GP clinics can clean minor wounds and give a tetanus booster. Deep or very dirty wounds may need an emergency department. Under the National Immunisation Programme, children get six doses of tetanus-containing vaccine, free at government clinics and schools: Age Vaccine 2, 3 and 5 months 6-in-1 vaccine (diphtheria, tetanus, whooping cough, polio, hepatitis B and Hib) 18 months 6-in-1 booster 7 years (Standard 1) DT (diphtheria and tetanus) 15 years (Form 3) Tetanus booster (ATT) Six doses give long-lasting protection. See our baby and child vaccination schedule . A booster about every 10 years keeps protection up. Doctors may use a vaccine against tetanus alone (ATT), tetanus and diphtheria (Td), or tetanus, diphtheria and whooping cough (Tdap). If you have never been vaccinated , or don’t know, you need a full course of 3 doses, spread over several months. Ask the doctor for the schedule. Older adults, gardeners, farmers, construction workers and people who travel to remote areas are especially worth checking. Keep a record of your last dose, for example in your phone, so you can answer the doctor’s question after an injury. Tetanus vaccination in pregnancy protects both the mother and the newborn baby, as tetanus can infect a baby’s umbilical cord stump after an unclean birth. Malaysia has vaccinated pregnant women against tetanus since 1976. Since 26 May 2025 , the Ministry of Health offers free Tdap to pregnant women, which also protects the baby against whooping cough in the first months of life. According to the government portal, women in their first pregnancy get a tetanus toxoid dose and a Tdap dose, and in later pregnancies a Tdap dose. It is given at Klinik Kesihatan, Klinik Desa and maternal and child health clinics. Tetanus vaccines are considered safe in pregnancy. Most people have no problems, or only a sore, red or swollen arm for a day or two, sometimes with a small lump at the injection site. Mild fever and tiredness are less common. Serious allergic reactions are very rare. Tell the doctor if you have reacted badly to a vaccine before. What is an ATT injection? ATT stands for anti-tetanus toxoid, the tetanus vaccine. In Malaysia the term is often used for any tetanus jab given after an injury or as a booster. Do I need a tetanus jab after stepping on a rusty nail? A puncture from a nail counts as a tetanus-prone wound. You need a booster if your last dose was 5 or more years ago, and may also need tetanus immunoglobulin if you were never fully vaccinated. How long does a tetanus injection last? After a full course, protection lasts about 10 years, which is why adults are advised to have a booster every 10 years. How soon after an injury do I need a tetanus injection? As soon as possible, ideally on the same day. If you missed that, it is still worth getting it later. Do I need a tetanus injection after a dog or cat bite? Bites are tetanus-prone wounds, so you may need a booster depending on your last dose. A doctor will also check whether you need rabies vaccination. What are the symptoms of tetanus? Jaw stiffness (lockjaw), a stiff neck, difficulty swallowing and painful muscle spasms, usually 3 to 21 days after the injury. It is an emergency. Is the tetanus vaccine safe in pregnancy? Yes. Malaysia gives pregnant women tetanus-containing vaccines, including free Tdap since May 2025, to protect the mother and baby. Where can I get a tetanus injection? At GP clinics and Klinik Kesihatan. For deep, very dirty or serious wounds, go to a hospital emergency department.

title: BMI calculator (Malaysia): check your BMI and healthy weight range
desc: Malaysia uses lower BMI cut-offs than many online calculators, because Asians face higher risks of diabetes and heart disease at a lower weight. Check your BMI, your healthy weight range and your waist with our free calculator, and learn what the numbers mean.
headings: BMI calculator · BMI categories for Malaysians · How to calculate BMI (cara kira BMI) · What is my ideal weight? (Berat badan ideal) · Why your waist matters too · Limits of BMI · Overweight and obesity in Malaysia · What to do if your BMI is high
keywords: Weight & metabolism BMI calculator Body mass index Obesity Berat badan ideal kencing manis gula hba1c darah tinggi hypertension bp tekanan darah mengandung hamil pregnancy antenatal klinik doctor doktor gp
body: BMI = your weight in kg divided by your height in metres, squared. Malaysian (Asian) cut-offs: under 18.5 is underweight, 18.5–22.9 is healthy, 23–27.4 is overweight and 27.5 or more is obese. International charts use 25 and 30. Malaysia uses lower cut-offs because Asians develop diabetes and heart disease at lower weights. A waist of 90 cm or more for men, or 80 cm or more for women, signals extra risk even at a healthy BMI. More than half of Malaysian adults are overweight or obese. Losing just 5–10% of your weight improves blood sugar, blood pressure and cholesterol. Enter your height in centimetres or feet and inches, and your weight in kilograms or pounds: use the small switches beside each label. Add your waist measurement if you know it. The calculator is for adults aged 18 and over. Height cm ft, in Weight kg lb Waist (cm, optional) Sex (for waist) Choose Female Male Calculate BMI For adults aged 18 and over, using the Malaysian BMI categories. Worked out in your browser: nothing you enter is stored or sent. This calculator needs JavaScript. To work out your BMI yourself, divide your weight in kg by your height in metres squared, or multiply your weight in pounds by 703 and divide by your height in inches squared. BMI (kg/m²) Malaysian category International (WHO) category Below 18.5 Underweight Underweight 18.5–22.9 Healthy weight Normal 23–24.9 Overweight Normal 25–27.4 Overweight Overweight 27.5–29.9 Obese Overweight 30 and above Obese Obese The Malaysian categories come from the Ministry of Health’s Clinical Practice Guidelines on the Management of Obesity (2nd edition, 2023). They follow a World Health Organization expert review, which found that Asian people have a high risk of type 2 diabetes and heart disease at BMIs below the international cut-off of 25. BMI = weight (kg) ÷ height (m) × height (m) In pounds and inches: BMI = 703 × weight (lb) ÷ height (in) × height (in) . Example: someone who weighs 70 kg and is 1.65 m tall: Height squared: 1.65 × 1.65 = 2.72 BMI: 70 ÷ 2.72 = 25.7 That counts as overweight under both the Malaysian and international cut-offs. The difference shows at lower and higher BMIs: a BMI of 24 looks “normal” on an international chart but counts as overweight in Malaysia, and a BMI of 28 counts as obese in Malaysia but only overweight internationally. There is no single “ideal” weight. A better guide is the healthy weight range for your height, which is the weight that gives a BMI between 18.5 and 22.9: Height Healthy weight range 150 cm 41.6–51.5 kg 155 cm 44.4–55.0 kg 160 cm 47.4–58.6 kg 165 cm 50.4–62.3 kg 170 cm 53.5–66.2 kg 175 cm 56.7–70.1 kg 180 cm 59.9–74.2 kg The calculator above works out the range for your exact height. Fat stored around the tummy is more harmful than fat elsewhere, raising the risk of type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure and heart disease. In Malaysia, a waist circumference of 90 cm or more for men or 80 cm or more for women counts as abdominal obesity, even if your BMI is in the healthy range. How to measure: stand up straight, breathe out normally, and wrap a tape measure around your middle halfway between your lowest rib and the top of your hip bone, usually around the belly button. Keep the tape snug but not tight. BMI is a useful first check, but it doesn’t measure body fat directly: Muscular people , such as athletes, can have a high BMI without excess fat. Older adults may have a normal BMI but less muscle and more fat. It isn’t suitable during pregnancy . Children and teenagers are assessed with BMI-for-age growth charts, which compare them with others of the same age and sex, not with the adult categories. A doctor can look at your BMI together with your waist, blood pressure, blood sugar and cholesterol for a fuller picture. The National Health and Morbidity Survey 2024 found that 53.6% of adults were overweight or obese (30.5% overweight and 23.1% obese), and more than half had abdominal obesity. Among children and teenagers aged 5 to 19, more than 1 in 4 were overweight or obese. These figures use international cut-offs, so more people would count under the Malaysian ones. Regular activity and small, lasting changes to eating habits are the foundation of healthy weight loss. Aim for 5–10% weight loss first. For someone weighing 80 kg, that is 4 to 8 kg. Even this much improves blood sugar, blood pressure and cholesterol. Eat smaller portions , especially of rice, noodles and bread, fill half your plate with vegetables, and cut down on sugary drinks, including teh tarik and sweetened kopi. Move more: aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate activity, such as brisk walking, each week. Get checked. A high BMI or waist is a reason to test your blood sugar, blood pressure and cholesterol. See our guides to normal blood sugar levels and blood pressure and cholesterol . Lifestyle change is the first step in the Malaysian obesity guideline. For people with a high BMI who haven’t lost enough weight with lifestyle changes alone, doctors may add weight-loss medicines, and bariatric surgery may be considered for a BMI of 37.5 or more, or 32.5 or more with conditions such as diabetes. See our guide to weight-loss injections . If your BMI is below 18.5 , or you have lost weight without trying, see a doctor to check for an underlying cause. What is a normal BMI in Malaysia? For adults, a healthy BMI in Malaysia is 18.5 to 22.9. A BMI of 23 to 27.4 is overweight and 27.5 or more is obese. How do I calculate my BMI? Divide your weight in kilograms by your height in metres squared. For example, 70 kg ÷ (1.65 m × 1.65 m) = 25.7. In pounds and inches, multiply your weight in pounds by 703 and divide by your height in inches squared. Why are Malaysian BMI cut-offs lower than international ones? Asian people tend to carry more body fat at the same BMI and develop diabetes and heart disease at lower weights, so Malaysia uses 23 and 27.5 instead of 25 and 30. What is my ideal weight for my height? The healthy range is the weight that gives a BMI of 18.5 to 22.9. For example, for someone 160 cm tall, that is about 47 to 59 kg. What waist size is too big? In Malaysia, a waist of 90 cm or more for men, or 80 cm or more for women, signals abdominal obesity and a higher risk of diabetes and heart disease. Is BMI accurate? It is a useful first check but doesn’t measure fat directly. It can overestimate fat in muscular people and underestimate it in older people, and isn’t used in pregnancy or for children. How much weight should I lose? Start with 5 to 10% of your current weight. That amount already improves blood sugar, blood pressure and cholesterol.

title: Medical certificates (MC) in Malaysia: sick leave rights, online MCs and the rules
desc: How many days of paid sick leave you get, the 48-hour rule for telling your employer, which doctors can issue an MC, why MCs from video consultations are no longer allowed, and the penalties for buying a fake MC.
headings: What is an MC? · How many days of sick leave do you get? · The 48-hour rule and panel clinics · Are online MCs valid? · Fake MCs: what the law says · Tips for getting an MC
keywords: Guides Medical certificate (MC) Medical certificate Sick leave Surat cuti sakit kecemasan emergency a&e hospital klinik doctor doktor gp
body: Under the Employment Act 1955, employees get 14 days of paid sick leave a year with less than 2 years’ service, 18 days with 2 to 5 years, and 22 days with 5 years or more, plus up to 60 days of hospitalisation leave. Since 1 January 2023, sick leave rights apply to all employees in Peninsular Malaysia and Labuan, whatever their salary. You must tell your employer within 48 hours of starting sick leave. If you don’t, the absence can be treated as unauthorised. An MC must be issued after the doctor has examined you. Since 2025, the Malaysian Medical Council doesn’t allow MCs issued only after a video or online consultation. Buying or using a fake MC is a crime under the Penal Code. Police recorded 33 cases from 2022 to March 2026. An MC (medical certificate, or sijil cuti sakit ) is a certificate from a doctor stating that you are unfit for work or school for a set period. In Malaysia it is often called an “MC chit”, meaning a short note. Your employer uses it to approve paid sick leave. A valid MC should show: your name and MyKad or passport number the date you were examined, and the dates of the sick leave the doctor’s signature, name and Malaysian Medical Council registration number the clinic’s details and a serial number Your diagnosis normally doesn’t need to be written on the MC, and should only be included with your consent. Under section 60F of the Employment Act 1955 , as amended in 2022: Length of service Paid sick leave a year Less than 2 years 14 days 2 to less than 5 years 18 days 5 years or more 22 days When admitted to hospital (or advised hospitalisation) Up to 60 days, on top of the above Since 1 January 2023 , these sick leave rights cover all employees in Peninsular Malaysia and Labuan, whatever their salary. Sick leave certified by a dental surgeon counts within your sick leave days. Many employers offer more than the legal minimum, so check your contract. In Sabah and Sarawak , sick leave comes under the state Labour Ordinances, which were amended from 1 May 2025 to add 60 days of hospitalisation leave. Tell your employer within 48 hours of the start of your sick leave. Under the Employment Act, sick leave that isn’t certified by a doctor, or isn’t notified within 48 hours, is treated as absence without permission. Being absent for more than 2 days in a row without telling your employer can be treated as breaking your contract. Who can issue the MC: a registered medical practitioner, including your company’s panel doctor or a government medical officer, or a dental surgeon. The doctor must examine you. Panel clinics: if your employer has appointed panel clinics, you are usually expected to use them. Check your company’s policy before seeing another doctor, for example if no panel clinic is open or nearby. Time slips are not MCs. A time slip (or attendance letter) only shows you visited a clinic, for example for a check-up. Whether it covers time off depends on your employer’s policy. Caring for a sick child: sick leave under the Employment Act is for your own illness. Time off to care for a sick child or family member depends on your employer’s policy, for example emergency or family care leave. Not if they are issued only after an online consultation. In a notification dated 23 September 2025, publicised in November 2025, the Malaysian Medical Council (MMC) said that issuing a medical certificate solely after a virtual consultation is not allowed , and doctors who do so face disciplinary action. Teleconsultation itself is still allowed: you can get advice, follow-up care and some prescriptions online. But to get an MC, you need to be examined in person . Be wary of websites or apps offering an MC through a quick online chat. MMC rules also say an MC must not be issued without a proper examination, pre-signed, or backdated except in special circumstances. A doctor who issues a false or misleading MC faces disciplinary action. An MC must be issued after the doctor has examined you in person. Buying, selling or using a fake MC is a criminal offence. Police have charged people under the Penal Code for cheating (section 420), forgery for the purpose of cheating (section 468) and using a forged document as genuine (section 471). These apply to buyers as well as sellers. Bukit Aman recorded 33 fake MC cases and 33 arrests from 2022 to March 2026, with 10 people charged in court. Most fake MCs were sold online. In June 2026, a government clinic nurse was among those arrested in Pekan, Pahang, over the sale of fake MCs. For employers: if you doubt an MC, contact the clinic named on it to check that it was issued. Don’t ask the clinic about the employee’s diagnosis, which is confidential. See a doctor on the day you fall ill, and bring your MyKad or passport, plus your company’s panel card if you have one. Ask the clinic for a copy if your employer needs one, and send a photo of the MC to your manager or HR straight away to meet the 48-hour rule. Many clinics are open in the evenings, at weekends and 24 hours, so you can be seen even if you fall ill outside office hours. If you are seriously unwell, don’t worry about the MC: go to a hospital emergency department or call 999 . See our guide on clinic or emergency department . How many days of MC can I take in a year? Under the Employment Act, 14 days with less than 2 years’ service, 18 days with 2 to 5 years and 22 days with 5 years or more, plus up to 60 days if you are hospitalised. Your contract may give more. Do I have to tell my employer about my MC? Yes, within 48 hours of the start of your sick leave. Otherwise the absence can be treated as unauthorised. Is an MC from an online consultation valid in Malaysia? No. The Malaysian Medical Council doesn’t allow doctors to issue an MC solely after a virtual consultation. You need to be examined in person. Can my employer reject an MC from a non-panel clinic? If your employer has panel clinics, you are usually expected to use them. Check your company policy, especially for times when no panel clinic is available. What does MC chit mean? It is an informal Malaysian and Singaporean term for a medical certificate, the doctor’s note that certifies you are unfit for work. Is a time slip the same as an MC? No. A time slip only shows you attended a clinic. It doesn’t certify that you were unfit for work, and how it is treated depends on your employer. What happens if I use a fake MC? It is a criminal offence. People who buy or use fake MCs have been charged under the Penal Code for cheating and forgery, and can also face dismissal.

title: Typhoid injection for food handlers in Malaysia: the rules, where to get it and how often
desc: Anyone who prepares or serves food in Malaysia must be vaccinated against typhoid and attend a food handler course. Who counts as a food handler, the penalties, how often the injection is repeated, where to get it, and what to expect.
headings: Do food handlers need a typhoid injection? What the law says · Who counts as a food handler? · How often do you need the typhoid injection? · Where to get a typhoid injection · The food handler course (kursus pengendali makanan) · About the typhoid vaccine: safety and side effects · What is typhoid?

body: Under the Food Hygiene Regulations 2009, every food handler must be medically examined and vaccinated, which in practice means the anti-typhoid injection, and must hold a food handler training certificate. Owners must not employ food handlers who aren’t trained and vaccinated, and must keep the records for inspection. Penalties go up to RM10,000 or 2 years in jail. Food handlers are usually asked to repeat the injection every 3 years. Some councils and clinics advise every 2 years, so check your local council’s rule. Private GP clinics give the typhoid injection, and some city councils run their own injection units. Bring your MyKad or passport. The injection is safe for most people. Side effects are usually a sore arm, mild fever or headache for a day or two. Yes. The Food Hygiene Regulations 2009 , made under the Food Act 1983, set three requirements: Training (regulation 30): every food handler must attend a food handler training course and hold a Certificate of Food Handlers Training from a training institution recognised by the Ministry of Health. Medical examination and vaccination (regulation 31): every food handler must be medically examined and vaccinated by a registered doctor. The Ministry of Health and local councils apply this as the anti-typhoid injection . Employers (regulation 11): the owner of food premises must not employ a food handler who hasn’t been trained and vaccinated, and must keep training and vaccination records for inspection. Each of these offences carries a penalty of up to RM10,000, up to 2 years in jail, or both , and can be settled with a compound. Food handlers who are ill with, or carry, an infection that can spread through food must report it and stop handling food until a doctor certifies them fit. Under the regulations, a food handler is anyone who prepares or serves food, or touches food, food equipment or surfaces that food touches, in food premises. That includes: cooks, kitchen helpers and dishwashers in restaurants, cafés and canteens hawkers, stall and food truck operators waiters and staff who serve or pack food workers in food factories, bakeries and catering businesses Local councils check typhoid and training records when you apply for or renew a food business licence, and health inspectors check them during inspections. In January to April 2026, for example, Penang health officers inspected more than 4,000 food premises and found workers without typhoid vaccination at seven of them. The injectable typhoid vaccine protects for about 3 years , so food handlers are usually asked to repeat it every 3 years . This is the interval the Ministry of Health has stated and many councils use. Some clinics and councils ask for a booster every 2 years, which matches international travel advice, so check what your local council requires when you renew your licence. Keep your typhoid injection card or record safe: you will need to show it to your employer and inspectors, and it tells you when the next dose is due. Private GP clinics: the most common option. Many give the injection on a walk-in basis and issue a card. It is worth calling ahead to check they have the vaccine in stock. City council injection units: some councils run their own service for food handlers, such as Kuala Lumpur City Hall’s (DBKL) injection unit and Johor Bahru City Council’s clinic. Check your council’s website for opening times and payment methods. Government health clinics: availability varies, so call your nearest Klinik Kesihatan before going. What to bring: your MyKad, or passport for foreign workers, and your food handler training certificate if you have one. Some councils also ask for a photo and your premises details. Cost: prices vary between clinics and councils, so ask when you call. Typhoid spreads through food and water contaminated by an infected person, which is why food handlers are vaccinated. The vaccination goes together with food handler training. The course is run by training schools recognised by the Ministry of Health, covers food hygiene, personal hygiene and food-borne diseases, and usually takes a few hours. Some recognised providers also run it online. Once you pass, you receive a certificate to show your employer and the local council. Ask your employer or local council which recognised training providers they accept. The typhoid injection used for food handlers is a single dose given in the upper arm. It can be given from age 2. Common side effects: pain, redness or swelling where the injection was given, mild fever, headache or feeling unwell for a day or two. Talk to the doctor first if you have had an allergic reaction to a vaccine before, are pregnant, or have a weakened immune system. If you are moderately or severely unwell on the day, the injection may be delayed. The vaccine is not 100% effective, so good hand-washing and food hygiene still matter. Newer typhoid conjugate vaccines, used in some countries from 6 months of age, give longer protection. Ask your doctor what is available. Typhoid fever is caused by the bacterium Salmonella Typhi, which only lives in humans. It spreads through food or water contaminated with the faeces of an infected person. Some people who recover keep carrying the bacteria and can pass it on through food they handle without feeling ill, which is why food handlers are screened and vaccinated. Symptoms include a prolonged high fever , tiredness, headache, stomach pain, constipation or diarrhoea, and sometimes a rash. Typhoid needs antibiotics, and drug resistance is increasingly common. In Malaysia it is a notifiable disease. Cases are relatively uncommon, but outbreaks have been traced to infected food handlers, such as one in Sabah in 2019 linked to a restaurant worker. See a doctor if you have a fever lasting more than 3 days, especially after eating from places with poor hygiene or travelling to areas where typhoid is common. For other causes of fever and food-borne illness, see our guides to dengue and stomach pain . Is the typhoid injection compulsory for food handlers in Malaysia? Yes. The Food Hygiene Regulations 2009 require food handlers to be medically examined and vaccinated, which is applied as the anti-typhoid injection, and to attend food handler training. How often do food handlers need a typhoid injection? Usually every 3 years, as the injectable vaccine protects for about 3 years. Some councils and clinics ask for every 2 years, so check with your local council. What is the fine for not having a typhoid injection? Food handlers who aren’t vaccinated, and owners who employ them, can be fined up to RM10,000, jailed for up to 2 years, or both. Offences can be compounded. Where can I get a typhoid injection? At private GP clinics, and at council injection units in some cities, such as DBKL in Kuala Lumpur and MBJB in Johor Bahru. Availability at government health clinics varies, so call ahead. Can foreign workers get the typhoid injection? Yes. Clinics give it to foreign food handlers too. Bring your passport. What are the side effects of the typhoid injection? Usually a sore arm, redness or swelling, and sometimes mild fever or headache for a day or two. Tell the doctor if you are pregnant, have a weak immune system or have had a vaccine allergy. Who counts as a food handler? Anyone who prepares, serves or touches food, food equipment or food-contact surfaces in food premises, including cooks, kitchen helpers, waiters, hawkers and food factory workers.

title: RSV in Malaysia: symptoms in babies and adults, danger signs, and the vaccine
desc: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) causes cold-like symptoms in most people but can make babies and older adults seriously ill. The symptoms, the breathing signs that need urgent care, how it is treated, and the vaccines and baby injections now available in Malaysia.
headings: What is RSV? · RSV symptoms in babies, children and adults · Who is at risk of severe RSV? · Is RSV the same as flu or COVID-19? · How RSV is treated · RSV vaccines and baby injections in Malaysia
keywords: Prevention RSV Respiratory syncytial virus Bronchiolitis kencing manis gula hba1c mengandung hamil pregnancy antenatal vaksin suntikan jab immunisation kecemasan emergency a&e hospital klinik doctor doktor gp aesthetic estetik kecantikan beauty kulit skin botox filler laser facial
body: RSV spreads through coughs, sneezes, touch and contaminated surfaces. Symptoms start 4 to 7 days after contact, and most people recover in 1 to 2 weeks. Babies under 6 months, premature babies, children with heart or lung conditions, older adults and people with weak immunity are most at risk of severe illness. Get urgent help if a baby is breathing fast or with effort, has pauses in breathing, blue or grey lips, is feeding much less or has no wet nappy for 12 hours. There is no specific medicine for RSV. Treatment is supportive: fluids, fever relief and, in hospital, oxygen. In Malaysia, RSV vaccines for adults aged 60+ and pregnant women, and a preventive antibody injection for babies, are available privately. They aren’t part of the free national programme. Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infects the nose, throat and lungs. It spreads through droplets from coughs and sneezes, by touching an infected person, and from contaminated hands, toys and surfaces, where it can survive for hours. Nearly all children have had RSV by age 2, and you can catch it again throughout life. RSV circulates all year in Malaysia, with peaks that often come in the second half of the year. A study of Negeri Sembilan’s government hospitals from 2017 to 2024 found that about 1 in 7 respiratory samples tested positive for RSV, with the usual peak between July and September. Symptoms usually start 4 to 7 days after catching the virus: Most children and adults: runny or blocked nose, cough, sneezing, sore throat, mild fever and tiredness, like a cold. Babies: may be irritable, feed less than usual and have less energy. Not all have a fever. RSV can spread to the small airways (bronchiolitis), causing a worsening cough, wheezing and fast or difficult breathing, often worst around days 3 to 5. Older adults: RSV can make heart and lung conditions such as asthma, COPD and heart failure worse, and can cause pneumonia or confusion. Most people recover within 1 to 2 weeks, although a cough can linger longer. See our guide to a cough that won’t go away . Get urgent medical help if a baby or child is breathing fast or working hard to breathe, with the skin pulling in under the ribs or at the neck; makes grunting noises or has pauses in breathing; has blue, grey or pale lips or tongue; is floppy, very sleepy or hard to wake; is feeding much less than usual or has had no wet nappy for 12 hours or more; is under 3 months old with a temperature of 38°C or above; or has a fit. Call 999 or go to an emergency department. babies under 6 months, especially in their first RSV season babies born prematurely children with heart or lung conditions, or a weakened immune system adults aged 60 or 75 and over, especially with long-term heart or lung disease or diabetes anyone with a weakened immune system No. RSV, influenza and COVID-19 are different viruses, but their symptoms overlap, so only a test can tell them apart. Some clinics and laboratories offer swab tests that check for several viruses at once. Knowing which virus it is can matter for high-risk people, as flu and COVID-19 have antiviral treatments while RSV doesn’t. See our guide to influenza A . RSV, flu and COVID-19 can all cause fever, cough and a runny nose. There is no specific antiviral medicine for RSV, and antibiotics don’t work against it. Most people can be cared for at home: Keep babies and children drinking: offer smaller, more frequent feeds. Use saline drops and gentle suction to clear a blocked nose before feeds. Give paracetamol (or ibuprofen for children old enough) for fever or discomfort, following the dose for their age. Don’t give aspirin to children under 16. Keep children away from cigarette smoke. Babies and adults who struggle to breathe or drink may need hospital care for oxygen, fluids and help clearing secretions. Several RSV prevention options have become available in Malaysia since 2024. None is yet part of the free National Immunisation Programme, so they are given at private clinics and hospitals. Who What is available Adults aged 60 and over RSV vaccines, given as a single dose. The first was approved in Malaysia in 2024. Pregnant women An RSV vaccine given in the third trimester, so the mother passes protective antibodies to her baby for the first months of life. Ask your obstetrician about the right timing. Babies A preventive antibody injection (nirsevimab), given as a single dose before or during a baby’s first RSV season. It has been available in Malaysia since November 2025. Doctors’ groups in Malaysia have called for RSV protection for babies to be added to the national programme. Until then, talk to your doctor or paediatrician about whether it is suitable for your family, especially for premature or high-risk babies. Also see our baby vaccination schedule . Everyday prevention: wash hands often, keep sick people away from young babies, avoid kissing babies on the face when you have a cold, clean toys and surfaces, and keep children with cold symptoms home from nursery. What are the symptoms of RSV in babies? A runny nose, cough, poor feeding, irritability and sometimes fever. In some babies it spreads to the lungs, causing wheezing and fast or difficult breathing. Get urgent help for breathing difficulty, pauses in breathing, blue lips or much reduced feeding. How long does RSV last? Most people recover in 1 to 2 weeks, though a cough can last longer. In babies, symptoms are often worst around days 3 to 5. Is RSV the same as flu? No. They are different viruses with similar symptoms, so only a test can tell them apart. Flu has antiviral treatments, while RSV doesn’t. How is RSV treated? There is no specific medicine. Treatment is supportive: fluids, fever relief, clearing a blocked nose and, for severe cases, oxygen and fluids in hospital. Is there an RSV vaccine in Malaysia? Yes. RSV vaccines are available privately for adults aged 60 and over and for pregnant women in the third trimester, and a preventive antibody injection is available for babies. They aren’t part of the free national programme. Is RSV contagious? Yes. It spreads through coughs, sneezes, touch and contaminated surfaces. People are usually infectious for 3 to 8 days, and young babies can spread it for longer.

title: Chickenpox (cacar air): symptoms, stages, how long it’s contagious, and the vaccine
desc: Chickenpox is usually mild in children but can be serious in adults, pregnant women and newborns. The symptoms and rash stages, how long to stay home, what eases the itch, which medicine to avoid, and the chickenpox vaccine in Malaysia.
headings: What is chickenpox? · Chickenpox symptoms and rash stages · How long is chickenpox contagious? · Home care: easing the itch and fever · When to see a doctor · Chickenpox in pregnancy · The chickenpox vaccine in Malaysia
keywords: Prevention Chickenpox Chickenpox Varicella Cacar air mengandung hamil pregnancy antenatal vaksin suntikan jab immunisation kecemasan emergency a&e hospital klinik doctor doktor gp aesthetic estetik kecantikan beauty kulit skin botox filler laser facial
body: Chickenpox is caused by the varicella-zoster virus. Spots appear 10 to 21 days after contact, usually around 2 weeks. It is contagious from 1 to 2 days before the rash until every blister has crusted over, usually about 5 days after the spots appear. Stay home until then. Use paracetamol for fever, and calamine, antihistamines and cool baths for itch. Don’t give ibuprofen unless a doctor advises it, and never give aspirin to children. Adults, pregnant women, newborns and people with weak immunity should see a doctor early, as antiviral medicine works best within 24 hours of the rash. The chickenpox vaccine is given as 2 doses from age 12 months. It isn’t in the free National Immunisation Programme, but private clinics offer it. Chickenpox is caused by the varicella-zoster virus , a member of the herpes family. It is also known in Malay as cacar air , and in some places as jintungan or bertih. It spreads very easily through coughs and sneezes, and by touching or breathing in virus from the fluid in the blisters. Most people only get chickenpox once and are then immune. But the virus stays in the body, and can wake up years later as shingles (kayap) . Symptoms appear 10 to 21 days after contact, usually about 2 weeks. A mild fever, aches, tiredness and loss of appetite often come a day or two before the rash. Then the spots go through stages: Red spots appear, often first on the face, scalp, chest, tummy or back, then spread over the body, sometimes inside the mouth. The spots fill with fluid to become very itchy blisters , which break within a day or two. The blisters dry into scabs , which fall off over 1 to 2 weeks. New spots keep appearing for a few days, so you often see spots, blisters and scabs at the same time. Chickenpox is usually milder in children and more severe in teenagers and adults, in whom pneumonia is the most common serious complication. In children, the most common complication is a bacterial skin infection from scratching. A person with chickenpox can spread it from 1 to 2 days before the rash appears until all the blisters have crusted over , usually about 5 days after the spots first appear. Keep your child home from nursery, kindergarten (tadika) or school, and stay off work yourself, until every spot has crusted. Keep away from pregnant women, newborn babies and people with weak immunity during this time. Paracetamol for fever and discomfort. Don’t give ibuprofen or other anti-inflammatory painkillers unless a doctor advises it, as they may raise the risk of serious skin infections with chickenpox. Never give aspirin to anyone under 16. Calamine lotion or cooling gels on the spots, and antihistamines from a pharmacy to reduce itching and help sleep. Bathing is fine and helps. A cool or lukewarm bath soothes itching. Pat the skin dry rather than rubbing. Keep nails short , and put socks or mittens on young children’s hands at night to stop scratching, which can cause infection and scars. Drink plenty of fluids , and wear loose cotton clothes. There is no need to follow special food restrictions (pantang). A normal, varied diet and plenty of fluids are best. Paracetamol is the safest choice for chickenpox fever. Avoid ibuprofen unless a doctor advises it. See a doctor within 24 hours of the rash appearing if you are an adult or teenager, pregnant, have a weakened immune system, or the person is a newborn baby. Antiviral medicine (aciclovir) can make chickenpox milder, but works best when started within 24 hours of the rash. Get urgent medical help if the skin around the blisters becomes red, hot, swollen or very painful; there is difficulty breathing or chest pain; a child is very drowsy, confused, has a stiff neck or a fit, or is showing signs of dehydration; or a newborn baby has chickenpox. Call 999 or go to an emergency department. Most women are already immune from childhood chickenpox. If you aren’t, chickenpox in pregnancy can cause pneumonia in the mother, and infection in the first 20 weeks carries a small risk (about 1–2%) of birth defects affecting the baby’s limbs, eyes or brain. Chickenpox around the time of delivery can make a newborn seriously ill. If you are pregnant and have been near someone with chickenpox or shingles, and you aren’t sure you have had chickenpox, see your doctor straight away . A blood test can check your immunity, and preventive treatment may be offered. Don’t wait for a rash. The chickenpox (varicella) vaccine is not part of Malaysia’s free National Immunisation Programme , but private clinics and hospitals offer it. It is given as 2 doses, from age 12 months . Ask your doctor about the interval between doses for your child’s age. Teenagers aged 13 and over and adults who have never had chickenpox also need 2 doses. Two doses are about 90% effective at preventing chickenpox, and those who still catch it usually have a much milder illness. Given within 3 to 5 days of contact with chickenpox, the vaccine can prevent or reduce illness in people who aren’t immune. Healthcare workers who aren’t immune are advised to be vaccinated. Paediatricians in Malaysia have called for the vaccine to be added to the national programme. Some countries have recently added it to their routine schedules, including the UK from January 2026. See also our baby vaccination schedule . What are the first signs of chickenpox? A mild fever, tiredness, aches and loss of appetite, followed within a day or two by red spots that turn into itchy, fluid-filled blisters, often starting on the face, chest or back. How long is chickenpox contagious? From 1 to 2 days before the rash appears until all the blisters have crusted over, usually about 5 days after the spots first appear. Can I bathe with chickenpox? Yes. A cool or lukewarm bath helps the itch. Pat the skin dry gently afterwards. Can I give ibuprofen for chickenpox? It is best to avoid ibuprofen unless a doctor advises it, as it may raise the risk of serious skin infections. Use paracetamol for fever, and never give aspirin to children. Is the chickenpox vaccine free in Malaysia? No. It isn’t in the National Immunisation Programme, but private clinics and hospitals offer it, given as 2 doses from age 12 months. Can you get chickenpox twice? It is uncommon. Most people are immune after one infection, but the virus stays in the body and can return later as shingles (kayap). Is chickenpox dangerous in pregnancy? It can be, if you aren’t immune. See a doctor straight away if you are pregnant and have been exposed, as preventive treatment may be offered.

title: Shingles (kayap): symptoms, is it contagious, treatment, myths and the vaccine
desc: Shingles, known in Malay as kayap, is chickenpox virus waking up years later. It causes a painful, one-sided band of blisters. The early signs, why you should see a doctor within 3 days, the truth about “kayap ular”, and the shingles vaccine now available in Malaysia.
headings: What is shingles (kayap)? · Shingles symptoms · Kayap ular, kayap sambung and other beliefs · Is shingles contagious? · Treatment: why the first 3 days matter · Nerve pain after shingles (post-herpetic neuralgia) · The shingles vaccine in Malaysia
keywords: Prevention Shingles (kayap) Shingles Herpes zoster Kayap mengandung hamil pregnancy antenatal vaksin suntikan jab immunisation klinik doctor doktor gp aesthetic estetik kecantikan beauty kulit skin botox filler laser facial
body: Shingles is the chickenpox virus (varicella-zoster) reactivating. Anyone who has had chickenpox can get it, and the risk rises after age 50 and with weak immunity. It usually starts with burning, tingling or pain on one side of the body, followed a few days later by a band of blisters that doesn’t cross the middle of the body. See a doctor within 3 days (72 hours) of the rash: antiviral medicine works best early and lowers the risk of long-lasting nerve pain. You can’t catch shingles, but blister fluid can give chickenpox to someone who isn’t immune. The belief that kayap kills if it “meets” around the body is a myth. A non-live shingles vaccine, given as 2 doses, has been available in Malaysia since 2024 for adults 50+ and adults 18+ at higher risk. After you have had chickenpox , the virus doesn’t leave your body. It lies dormant in nerve roots near the spine, sometimes for decades. If it reactivates, it travels along a nerve to the skin and causes shingles (herpes zoster), called kayap in Malay. Anyone who has had chickenpox can get shingles. It becomes more common after age 50 , and in people whose immunity is weakened by illness, cancer treatment or medicines such as steroids. Stress is often blamed, but age and immunity are the main factors. In the United States, about 1 in 3 people get shingles during their lifetime. Before the rash: burning, tingling, itching or sharp pain in one area of skin, sometimes with a headache, fever or feeling unwell. This can last a few days and is easily mistaken for a pulled muscle or, on the chest, heart pain. The rash: a red rash that turns into clusters of fluid-filled blisters, in a band or patch on one side of the body , most often around the chest or waist. It doesn’t usually cross the middle of the body. Healing: the blisters scab over in 7 to 10 days, and the rash usually clears in 2 to 4 weeks. See a doctor urgently if the rash is on your face near the eye or on the tip of your nose, or you have eye pain, redness or blurred vision, as shingles can damage the eye; you have weakness on one side of your face, ear pain or hearing problems (Ramsay Hunt syndrome); the rash is widespread or on both sides of the body; or you have a weakened immune system. Kayap is surrounded by folk beliefs in Malaysia: “Kayap ular” describes the snake-like band of the rash. It is ordinary shingles, not a different disease. “If the kayap meets around the body, you will die” (kayap sambung): a myth. The shingles rash follows a single nerve on one side of the body, so it doesn’t encircle the body. Shingles is painful and troublesome, but in most people it isn’t life-threatening. A rash that spreads widely or appears on both sides is rare and suggests a weakened immune system. It needs prompt medical care for that reason, not because the ends “meet”. Names such as “kayap api” or “kayap air” are traditional descriptions, not separate medical conditions. Relying on traditional remedies alone can mean missing the 3-day window for antiviral treatment. Applying pastes or herbs to open blisters can also cause infection. See a doctor first. You can’t catch shingles from someone with shingles. But the fluid in the blisters contains the virus , and can give chickenpox to someone who has never had chickenpox or the vaccine. The risk is only while there are open blisters. Once they have scabbed over, you can’t pass it on. Keep the rash covered, don’t touch or scratch it, and wash your hands often. Until the blisters have crusted, avoid pregnant women who haven’t had chickenpox, babies under 1 month old and people with weak immunity. Antiviral medicines (such as aciclovir, valaciclovir or famciclovir) can shorten the illness and reduce the risk of complications. They work best when started within 72 hours (3 days) of the rash appearing, so don’t wait to see if it gets better. Take pain relief as advised by your doctor or pharmacist. Keep the rash clean and dry, and wear loose cotton clothing. Cool, damp compresses can ease discomfort. A two-dose shingles vaccine has been available in Malaysia since 2024. The most common complication is post-herpetic neuralgia (PHN) : burning, stabbing or aching pain in the area of the rash that continues for months, or even years, after the rash heals. It is more likely in people over 50, people with weakened immunity, and those who start antivirals late. Ordinary painkillers often don’t help nerve pain. Doctors may prescribe medicines for nerve pain, numbing skin patches, or refer you to a pain clinic. Tell your doctor if pain continues after the rash has gone. A non-live (recombinant) shingles vaccine has been available in Malaysia since September 2024. Who: adults aged 50 and over , and adults aged 18 and over with a higher risk, such as weakened immunity from illness or treatment. Doses: 2 injections, given 2 to 6 months apart (1 to 2 months apart for people with weakened immunity). Protection: about 97% effective in people aged 50 to 69 and 91% in those 70 and over, with strong protection lasting at least 7 years. It also greatly reduces the risk of post-herpetic neuralgia. You can have it even if you have had shingles before, once the rash has gone. The shingles vaccine isn’t part of a free government programme, so it is given at private clinics and hospitals. Ask your doctor whether it is right for you. What are the first signs of shingles (kayap)? Burning, tingling, itching or pain on one side of the body, followed a few days later by a band of red blisters in the same area. Some people also have a headache or fever. Is shingles contagious? You can’t catch shingles itself, but fluid from the blisters can give chickenpox to someone who isn’t immune. Keep the rash covered until the blisters have crusted. Is it true kayap kills if it meets around the body? No. This is a myth. The shingles rash follows one nerve on one side of the body and doesn’t encircle the body. A widespread rash is rare and needs prompt care because it suggests weakened immunity. How soon should I see a doctor for shingles? Within 3 days (72 hours) of the rash appearing, when antiviral medicine works best. See a doctor urgently if the rash is near your eye. How long does shingles last? The blisters crust in 7 to 10 days and the rash usually clears in 2 to 4 weeks. Some people have nerve pain for months afterwards. Is there a shingles vaccine in Malaysia? Yes. A non-live, 2-dose shingles vaccine has been available since 2024 for adults 50 and over and adults 18 and over at higher risk. It is given at private clinics and hospitals. Can you get shingles more than once? Yes, although it is uncommon. The vaccine can be given after a past episode, once the rash has gone.

title: Appendicitis: symptoms, which side the appendix is on, and when to go to hospital
desc: Pain that starts around the belly button and moves to the lower right side can be appendicitis, a common surgical emergency. The signs to watch for, when the appendix can burst, how doctors diagnose it, and what treatment and recovery involve.
headings: What is appendicitis? · Which side is the appendix on? · Symptoms of appendicitis (tanda appendix) · Can the appendix burst? · What to do if you think it’s appendicitis · How appendicitis is diagnosed · Treatment: surgery or antibiotics? · Recovery after appendix surgery
keywords: Guides Appendicitis Appendicitis Apendisitis mengandung hamil pregnancy antenatal kecemasan emergency a&e hospital klinik doctor doktor gp aesthetic estetik kecantikan beauty kulit skin botox filler laser facial
body: The appendix is a small pouch attached to the large intestine on the lower right side of the abdomen. About 5 to 9 in 100 people get appendicitis at some point, most often in their teens and 20s. The classic pattern is pain around the belly button that moves to the lower right within hours, gets worse when you move or cough, with loss of appetite, nausea and fever. Children, pregnant women and older people often have milder or unusual symptoms. An inflamed appendix can burst within 1 to 2 days, causing a serious infection. Go to an emergency department if you suspect appendicitis, and call 999 if pain is severe and spreading. The usual treatment is keyhole surgery to remove the appendix, with recovery in 1 to 2 weeks. You don’t need your appendix to live normally. The appendix (apendiks) is a small, finger-shaped pouch attached to the large intestine. Appendicitis means it has become inflamed, usually because it is blocked, for example by hardened stool, and then infected. It is common: about 5 to 9 in every 100 people have appendicitis during their life. It can happen at any age, but is most common in children over 10, teenagers and young adults, and is slightly more common in males. It is rare in babies. The appendix is on the lower right side of the abdomen (bawah kanan perut), roughly between your belly button and the bony point at the front of your right hip. That is where appendicitis pain usually settles. Pain on the lower left side is rarely appendicitis. It has other causes, which we cover in our guide to stomach pain by location . In pregnancy, the growing womb can push the appendix higher, so the pain may be felt higher up on the right. The classic pattern: Pain starts in the middle , around the belly button. It may come and go at first. Within hours it moves to the lower right side, becomes constant and gets steadily worse. Moving, coughing, walking or going over bumps in a car makes it hurt more. Other common symptoms are loss of appetite , feeling sick or vomiting, a fever , constipation or diarrhoea, and needing to urinate more often. Not everyone has the classic pattern. In young children, pregnant women and older people, pain can be milder, come on more slowly or be felt somewhere else. Older people may simply become confused. Children may be unusually quiet, refuse food or not want to walk. Call 999 or go to an emergency department now if the pain suddenly spreads across your whole abdomen, or gets much worse after briefly easing; you have a high fever, a fast heartbeat, pale or blotchy skin, or difficulty breathing; or you feel confused or faint. These can be signs that the appendix has burst. Don’t drive yourself. Yes. If appendicitis isn’t treated, the inflamed appendix can burst (appendix pecah), often within 1 to 2 days of the first symptoms. This spills infection into the abdomen (peritonitis) and can lead to an abscess or sepsis, which are life-threatening and need more complex surgery and a longer hospital stay. The pain may ease for a short while when the appendix bursts, as the pressure is released, before becoming severe and spreading. Don’t take an easing of pain as a sign you are getting better. Go to a hospital emergency department if you have pain that has moved to the lower right side and is getting worse. A GP can assess milder or unclear tummy pain and refer you if needed, but for typical appendicitis symptoms go straight to hospital. Don’t wait it out overnight hoping it will settle. Avoid eating or drinking until you have been seen, in case you need an operation. Bring a list of any medicines you take, and tell the doctor if you could be pregnant. Not sure where to go? See our guide on clinic or emergency department . There is no single test for appendicitis. A doctor will: ask about your symptoms and press on your abdomen to find where it is tender do blood tests (to look for signs of infection) and a urine test (to rule out a urine infection or kidney stone), plus a pregnancy test for women often arrange an ultrasound (commonly used for children and pregnant women) or a CT scan Doctors may use a scoring system such as the Alvarado score , which adds points for symptoms, tenderness and blood results. A low score makes appendicitis unlikely, and a high score makes it probable. If the picture isn’t clear, you may be observed in hospital for a few hours, or up to a day, to see how symptoms change. Diagnosis combines an examination, blood and urine tests, and often a scan. The standard treatment is an operation to remove the appendix, called an appendicectomy (appendectomy), usually done as soon as possible. Most are done by keyhole (laparoscopic) surgery through a few small cuts, and take about an hour. Open surgery through a larger cut may be needed if the appendix has burst. Antibiotics instead of surgery? For some adults with uncomplicated appendicitis confirmed on a scan, antibiotics alone are an option. Large trials found that about 3 in 10 people treated with antibiotics needed their appendix removed within a year, rising to about 4 in 10 within five years, and the risk was higher when a hardened stool stone (appendicolith) was present. Your surgeon will explain whether this is suitable for you. After keyhole surgery, many people go home the next day. Recovery after a burst appendix or open surgery takes longer. Most people need 1 to 2 weeks off work or school, and should avoid heavy lifting and strenuous sport for a few weeks until fully healed. Get medical advice if you develop a fever, increasing pain or swelling, redness or discharge from a wound, or vomiting after going home. Can you live without an appendix? Yes. Removing it doesn’t cause any long-term problems. What are the first signs of appendicitis? Usually a dull pain around the belly button that moves to the lower right side within hours and gets worse, especially when moving or coughing, with loss of appetite, nausea and sometimes fever. Which side is the appendix on? The lower right side of the abdomen. In pregnancy the pain may be felt higher up on the right, because the womb pushes the appendix upwards. How long before the appendix bursts? It varies, but an inflamed appendix can burst within 1 to 2 days of the first symptoms. That is why suspected appendicitis needs to be seen in hospital the same day. Can appendicitis go away on its own? Pain may ease temporarily, but appendicitis needs medical treatment.
